title: NY Giants to start J.J. McCarthy against the Houston Texans
summary: The New York Giants are planning to start J.J. McCarthy against the Houston Texans, per a report from ESPN. Head coach John Harbaugh confirmed that decision after Wednesday’s practice. The Giants traded a fifth-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings for McCarthy following the injury that cost Jaxson Dart his season. The former 10th overall pick […]
full_text: J.J. McCarthy | Getty Images The New York Giants are planning to start J.J. McCarthy against the Houston Texans, per a report from ESPN . Head coach John Harbaugh confirmed that decision after Wednesday’s practice. The Giants traded a fifth-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings for McCarthy following the injury that cost Jaxson Dart his season. The former 10th overall pick was a backup and package player for the Giants until he was put on the field in place of Jameis Winston following the latter’s second interception against the Saints. McCarthy nearly led the Giants on a furious comeback, but while he didn’t win the game, he seems to have won the chance to start. McCarthy was considered a potential pick for the Giants at No. 6 overall in the 2024 NFL Draft, but New York ultimately chose wide receiver Malik Nabers out of LSU. Instead, the Vikings traded up from 11th overall to secure the rights to draft McCarthy out of Michigan with the 10th overall pick. McCarthy wasn’t a high-volume passer at Michigan under Jim Harbaugh, however he did have a reputation as a smart quarterback who performed well in high-leverage situations. McCarthy and Nabers showed an immediate rapport once McCarthy took the field in the fourth quarter against the Saints. The two connected for receptions of 46, 27, 13, and 9 yards, accounting for 95 of Nabers’ 165 yards on the day. The decision to start McCarthy is likely due in part to the Giants’ struggles running the ball. Their offense was designed from the start with Jaxson Dart in mind and, like Dart, McCarthy is a highly athletic quarterback who’s able to add an explosive dimension to their backfield. McCarthy is also a much more mobile passer and has a stronger arm than Winston. He’s better able stress to defenses by extending the play, as well as stretch them vertically to prevent them from playing downhill. The Giants are clearly hoping that, in addition to Winston’s limitations becoming increasingly apparent, McCarthy can spark the Giants’ offense and allow it to function as intended. McCarthy’s first start comes as the Giants face a stiff test against the Houston Texans. The Giants are currently 9.5-point underdogs (per FanDuel) as they try to rebound from their loss against the Saints. Let us know if you agree with the decision in the comments below.
author: Chris Pflum

title: 3 storylines for NY Giants vs. Houston Texans: Will it be Jameis or J.J. at QB?
summary: The biggest storyline of the week heading into the New York Giants Week 7 game vs. the Houston Texans is whether the Giants will start Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy at quarterback. Giants head coach John Harbaugh wasn’t ready to decide on Sunday night after McCarthy’s fourth-quarter heroics nearly brought the Giants back from a […]
full_text: The biggest storyline of the week heading into the New York Giants Week 7 game vs. the Houston Texans is whether the Giants will start Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy at quarterback. Giants head coach John Harbaugh wasn’t ready to decide on Sunday night after McCarthy’s fourth-quarter heroics nearly brought the Giants back from a 24-point deficit in a 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. On Monday, he said the team was still “honing in” on a decision. Theoretically, Harbaugh does not have to announce a decision on Wednesday. It would seem logical, though, since this is the beginning of the practice week and reporters will see which quarterback takes the first reps during individual drills early in practice. Fans who voted in our ‘Jameis or J.J.?’ poll clearly want McCarthy to start. Do the Giants stay with Winston’s experience and his knowledge of the offense? It is a frustrating ride with Winston, but the Giants have lost one time in his four starts this season, and as a captain and member of the team’s Leadership Council, it is clear how much respect his teammates have for him. Do they venture into the unknown with McCarthy, and perhaps risk upsetting what has thus far been a mostly harmonious locker room? McCarthy gives them mobility that allows them to expand their playbook, and maybe untapped upside at just 23 years of age. Still, it is important to remember that despite his impressive relief performance on Sunday, the Giants were able to get McCarthy because a team with a shaky quarterback situation had him as QB3 and was happy to be rid of him. Getting going on the ground The Giants’ offense was built to be a physical, run-first attack that would take some pressure off quarterback Jaxson Dart and wear down opposing defenses. Unfortunately, the Giants have not run the ball well. They average 3.8 yards per attempt, 22nd in the league. That number isn’t even a true picture of how ineffective the run game has been. It is inflated by a 28-yard J.J. McCarthy scramble, a 22-yard Dart run, and a 20-yard Darnell Mooney reverse. The Giants do not have a 20-yard run from a running back this season. They average 3.9 yards per attempt when giving the ball to a back, with Cam Skattebo’s 3.6 yards per rush topping the list. The backs and the blocking have both been problematic. Getting more production out of the run game is a must, and part of the Winston-McCarthy equation. The backs Harbaugh said the other day that he would love to have a Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley circumstance, with a clear No. 1 stud running back. Hopefully, nobody reminds Harbaugh that one of those guys was a Giant. Go back to the offseason. The Giants were interested in free agent running back Kenneth Walker before he signed with the Kansas City Chiefs. They were thought to be seriously considering using the No. 5 overall pick on running back Jerimiyah Love. It is clear they felt they needed more at running back. It is why they took a chance with Harris, a four-time 1,000-yard rusher. That didn’t pan out. quarterback situation had him as QB3 and was happy to be rid of him. Skattebo is more bulldozer than big-play, breakaway back. With four fumbles in five games (the sixth doesn’t count since he never touched the ball), he has clearly lost some trust. Tracy is a slasher and a good pass receiver. Of the current backs the Giants have, trying to get him more carries might be the Giants’ best chance to create more explosive runs. We know they need them: Singletary is Mr. Consistency. He won’t make mistakes as a pass protector, and he has just four fumbles in 1,352 career touches. Going forward, it won’t surprise me if Singletary becomes the back the Giants close games with while trying to protect a lead. The blocking Watch the Giants try to run the football, and you too often see a block that doesn’t get executed. Harris’s 6-yard loss Sunday against the New Orleans Saints was a perfect example. He lost those yards because Jon Runyan Jr. got knocked into him about 4 yards behind the line of scrimmage. Harris had no chance on the play. Pro Football Focus grades and Pro Football and Sports Network Impact scores are not perfect indicators of performance. But they can tell us some things. An average PFF grade is 60.0. The Giants’ team run-blocking grade is 49.5, 29th in the league. Only one regular player, right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (83.9), has been well above average as a run blocker. Fullback Patrick Ricard (55.6) and offensive linemen Runnyan (54.3), John Michael Schmitz (50.5), and Sisi Mauigoa (50.0) have been below average. Marcus Mbow is at 45.2 in limited duty. An average PFSN Impact Score is 75.0. The Giants’ team run-blocking score is 69.0, 26th. Only Giants’ offensive linemen have played enough snaps to qualify for a PFSN Impact Score. In run-blocking, Andrew Thomas (78.6) and Eluemunor (77.2) are slightly above average. Mauigoa 67.8) and Runyan (63.7) are well below average. Mauigoa is having a rocky start to his career. Runyan is an excellent pass blocker, but a poor run blocker. Thomas is playing hurt. Eluemunor is now hurt. Bryan Hudson has replaced Schmitz at center, and it is too early to tell whether or not he is the answer at center. Blame whoever and whatever you want, but too often Giants’ running backs have had no chance. Beating themselves The Giants are a team that does not have a huge margin for error. Four of their five games this season have been either one-score games or decided in the closing seconds. The Giants have two victories courtesy of game-saving interceptions by Jevon Holland and Deonte Banks. Unfortunately, the Giants have a tie and a loss in the last two weeks that their own mistakes are to blame for. Over six games, the Giants have actually made a shocking number of self-inflicted, sometimes undisciplined mistakes. The Giants have fumbled 11 times. Only the Los Angeles Rams (13) have more fumbles. The Giants have lost seven of those fumbles. Add in four interceptions thrown by Giants quarterbacks, and New York has 11 turnovers. Only five teams have more. Overall, the Giants are -2 in takeaway/giveaway ratio. Penalties have also been a problem. The Giants have 46, and only 11 teams have more. Twenty-four of those penalties have been pre-snap. Only the Cleveland Browns (29) have more pre-snap infractions. The Giants have only five special teams penalties, the fifth-fewest in the NFL. Unfortunately, four of those came last week in the second half against the Saints. Those penalties negated punt returns by Charlie Jones of 32, 15, 33, and 9 yards. Beating themselves is something the Giants have to stop doing.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 7
summary: No. 1 — San Francisco 49ers (6-0) | SAME San Francisco remains the NFL’s hottest and most dangerous team. full_text: Matthew Stafford of the Rams and Josh Allen of the Bills. | Getty Images No. 1 — San Francisco 49ers (6-0) | SAME San Francisco remains the NFL’s hottest and most dangerous team. They play complementary football, and Brock Purdy is playing like one of the league’s best quarterbacks right now. No. 2 —Buffalo Bills (5-1) | SAME Buffalo traveled across the country and defeated a good Raiders team. Josh Allen threw for 255 yards with two touchdowns, including a crucial one to Keon Coleman. The 49ers and Bills remain the top two teams in the league. No. 3 — Kansas City Chiefs (5-0) | SAME Kansas City came out of the BYE week and beat up the lifeless Los Angeles Chargers, 22-6. The rushing attack continues to spearhead the Chiefs offense; Kenneth Walker III ran for 128 yards and scored two touchdowns to help secure the win. No. 4 — Minnesota Vikings (5-0) | SAME Minnesota had a BYE in Week 6. No. 5 — Chicago Bears (4-2) | (10th) 📈 5 spots Caleb Williams returned and was efficient, completing 30 of 36 for 305 yards and a touchdown in Atlanta. The Falcons made it more interesting in the fourth quarter, but the Bears still escaped with a 31-23 victory. No. 6 — New England Patriots (4-2) (9th) | 📈 3 spots New England defeated the Jets, 26-19. The game was tight, but Drake Maye — who has played much better the last three weeks — found victory. No. 7 — Denver Broncos (4-2) | (15th) 📈 8 spots It doesn’t always look pretty — especially on offense — but a 17-14 victory against the Super Bowl champions is worth something. Sam Darnold threw two critical late interceptions that ended the Seahawks’ chances for a comeback, despite Jaxon Smith-Njigba’s 12 catches for 134 yards. No. 8 —Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) | (7th) 📉 1 spot Liam Coen’s offense dropped 31 points against the Texans in London. No. 11 — Green Bay Packers (4-2) | (17th) 📈 6 spots Green Bay beat up the Cowboys, 23-13. Both Matthew Golden and Christian Watson were creating a bunch of separation, but their hands failed them multiple times; still, Golden went north of 100 yards on six catches, and Watson had 64 yards on three catches. The Packers’ defense stifled the Cowboys; Dak Prescott threw 54 passes in the game, and the end result was just 13 points. No. 12— Carolina Panthers | (13th) 📈 1 spots The Panthers went into Philadelphia and handled a very injured Eagles team, 25-14. Bryce Young threw for 281 yards with a pair of touchdowns, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards with a score. No. 13 — Detroit Lions (3-2) | (12th) 📉 1 spot The Lions had their BYE in Week 6 No. 14 — Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) | SAME The Pittsburgh Steelers escaped Tampa Bay with a 26-19 win, where the Buccaneers’ Jalon Daniels had a last-minute drive that Pittsburgh’s defense stopped. Aaron Rodgers threw for 253 yards with two touchdowns and an interception, as rookie receiver Germie Bernard caught 11 passes for 87 yards with a score. No. 15 — Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) | (11th) 📉 4 spots The Bengals were BYE in Week 6 No. 16 —Cleveland Browns (4-2) | (22nd) 📈 6 spots The Browns won a classic, low-scoring 13-10 game over the Tyler Huntley-led Baltimore Ravens. Audric Esteme — who was signed earlier that week off the Vikings’ practice squad — ran in the go-ahead touchdown. Cleveland had two healthy backs and won with 164 passing yards; Jaleel McLaughlin led the rushing attack with just 41 yards. No. 17 — Los Angeles Rams (2-4) | (5th) 📉 12 spots The Rams were beaten by a six-field-goal effort off the foot of Chad Ryland. The Rams could not get much going against the Cardinals’ defense. The Rams totaled just 286 yards. A game to forget for a now sub-.500 Rams. No. 18 — Houston Texans (2-4) | (21st) 📈 3 spots The Texans defeated the Jaguars with a last-second field goal and are now on a two-game winning streak after starting 0-4. They host the Giants in Week 7. No. 19 — Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) | (16th) 📉 4 spots Kirk Cousins threw for 313 yards and two touchdowns, but also threw an interception. Tre Tucker had five catches for 97 yards with a pair of touchdowns. Michael Mayer led the tight ends with seven catches for 95 yards on nine targets. The Raiders have now lost three straight games — when will we see Francisco Mendoza? No. 20 — New York Giants (3-2-1) | (18th) 📉 2 spots The Giants are entertaining a QB question, but J.J. McCarthy sparked an impressive comeback effort that fell short. The Giants can’t run the football at all, and their ability to stop the run failed them against the Saints in the third quarter. However, their defense has a clear identity, and Malik Nabers/Isaiah Likely are playing out of their mind. They’re a resilient, competitive team, but they have serious question marks. title: NY Giants news: Najee Harris, Jihad Ward cut, QB1 decision day, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as John Harbaugh get set to announce their starting quarterback for Sunday. There doesn’t need to be an immediate urgency for Giants’ QB decision | New York Post There must be urgency. A sense of urgency. An emphasis on urgency. Urgency […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as John Harbaugh get set to announce their starting quarterback for Sunday. There doesn’t need to be an immediate urgency for Giants’ QB decision | New York Post There must be urgency. A sense of urgency. An emphasis on urgency. Urgency for this upcoming practice. Urgency for the next game. The offense must have urgency. The defense must have urgency. Urgency for all. What is probably inevitable does not need to happen right now. What’s the urgency to replace Jameis Winston with J.J. McCarthy? The upcoming schedule offers a smarter option if a change is to be made. DJ Reader: Division is there for us to win "I think that's kind of how you've got to look at it – somebody's got to go take it and we should be the ones to go do that." DJ Reader talks about the Giants leading the NFC East and how important it is to take advantage of other teams losing: pic.twitter.com/HU3SKBw2TV — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 20, 2026 Jameis Winston vs. J.J. McCarthy: Pros and cons of Giants ’ QBs | ESPN.com The element of the unknown is perhaps McCarthy’s most attractive trait. He has talent as a top-10 pick of the Minnesota Vikings in 2024, and who knows, there might be high-end quarterback play buried somewhere in there. At the very least, McCarthy flashed that potential in his short stint Sunday. It was impressive. So was McCarthy’s ability to throw the ball deep downfield. He went 3-of-4 for 119 yards with a touchdown and no interceptions on passes of 20 air yards or more. Winston did not attempt any such passes against the Saints. Harbaugh said he would judge the quarterbacks based on “performance.” And it’s hard to argue what McCarthy did leading the Giants on three scoring drives and close to a fourth even though it was in a helter-skelter football circumstance trying to rally in the final minutes. McCarthy could also provide a much-needed boost to the running game. The Giants designed an offense for Dart filled with zone-reads and quarterback rollouts. That’s better suited to McCarthy’s game than Winston’s. Harbaugh conceded that. Were Giants QB J.J. McCarthy’s late-game heroics real or a product of ‘desperation time’? | The Athletic McCarthy’s arm talent was never in doubt, and he delivered a highlight reel’s worth of impressive throws in a short period. But the Saints played very conservatively as they tried (unsuccessfully) to guard against big plays. They sent four rushers almost exclusively and played soft zone coverage. That was a change from the first half when the Saints crowded the line of scrimmage and mixed blitzes at Winston on passing downs. It will be much different if McCarthy has to play a full game against the Texans’ defense, which hasn’t played up to its standard but still has elite talent, led by All-Pro defensive ends Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter. A key factor in McCarthy’s favor is that he has enough athleticism that opponents must respect the quarterback runs that were a staple of the playbook with Dart. The struggle to establish the run has been a source of immense frustration for Harbaugh. Jameis Winston should be Giants’ starter, but John Harbaugh may go to J.J. McCarthy | New York Daily News Harbaugh needs to steady this ship, not keep running out a different captain every few weeks hoping the change will sprinkle magic pixie dust over the rest of the crew. The first-place Giants (3-2-1) have Sunday’s game against the Texans, a bye and then two NFC East tilts away at the Eagles (2-4) and at home against the Commanders (1-3-1 entering Monday night). Regardless of what happens in Houston, if the Giants beat Philly and Washington after the bye, they would be 3-0-1 in the division entering the back half of the regular season. Winning those division games should be the priority. And frankly, so far, Harbaugh has empowered Winston as this team’s North star since Dart’s season-ending injury. So pivoting hard to McCarthy this quickly could give this uncertain Giants locker room some whiplash at a time when they seem a bit fragile and beaten up. The 11 Biggest Overreactions After NFL Week 6 | Bleacher Report J.J. McCarthy Can Revive the New York Giants’ Offense. Seeing McCarthy on the field during a meaningful contest less than a month after he joined the team shows just how desperate the G-Men are. With Winston reverting to his turnover-prone ways—tossing a pair of picks that effectively put the game out of reach—the coaching staff elected to see what it had in the third-year backup. Although McCarthy racked up 243 passing yards in short order, he also struggled with accuracy (completing just 11 of 21 passes) and turnovers (tossing an interception on his first drive). Those same issues doomed McCarthy’s chances of leading the Minnesota Vikings and will prevent him from becoming a quality starter in the Big Apple. If McCarthy does usurp Winston as the starter going forward, the G-Men will remain a fringe playoff team at best with no real shot at contending for anything beyond a Wild Card appearance. Tiki: Teammates want Jameis to start this week Evan and Tiki both believe Giants players likely prefer Jameis Winston to start over J.J. McCarthy: @EvanRobertsWFAN pic.twitter.com/n9yyc7S2ou — WFAN Sports Radio (@WFAN660) October 20, 2026 Jameis Winston ’ s Super Surprise For Breast Cancer Survivors: ‘ Nothing Short Of Amazing ’ | FOX Sports Helping breast cancer survivors has become a passion for Winston, who has held an annual event at games since he was with the New Orleans Saints in the early 2020s. He was inspired by the stories of his Aunt Lois in Birmingham, Alabama, and his Aunt De-De and cousin Tonda in Louisville, Kentucky, who are all survivors of the terrible disease. “It’s one of the most rewarding things I get to do,” Winston told me. “We want to give these women a special experience, but every year I feel like I’m the one walking away blessed. title: Aaron Glenn’s praise of Frank Reich invites scrutiny
summary: After the Jets’ Week 6 loss to the Patriots, offensive coordinator Frank Reich has been a target of fan and media criticism for his playcalling. Head coach Aaron Glenn said positive things about Reich’s performance to the media on Wednesday. Asked if the offensive struggles might prompt him to get more involved in helping Frank […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - OCTOBER 18: Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets during a game between the New England Patriots and the New York Jets on October 18, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After the Jets’ Week 6 loss to the Patriots, offensive coordinator Frank Reich has been a target of fan and media criticism for his playcalling. Head coach Aaron Glenn said positive things about Reich’s performance to the media on Wednesday. Asked if the offensive struggles might prompt him to get more involved in helping Frank Reich, Aaron Glenn said he's always collaborating with his coordinators on ways to improve. He also said we should "acknowledge" some of the positives on offense. He mentioned their explosive… — Rich Cimini (@RichCimini) October 21, 2026 Asked if the offensive struggles might prompt him to get more involved in helping Frank Reich, Aaron Glenn said he’s always collaborating with his coordinators on ways to improve. He also said we should “acknowledge” some of the positives on offense. He mentioned their explosive plays on play-action (six pass plays of 20+ yards, T-9th) and an improved run game (12th in rushing over last two weeks). #Jets Glenn noting explosive plays off play action in combination with the run game is interesting to me. Many offensive coordinators effectively build their deep passing game off their run game and play action. And according to the advanced stats at Pro Football Reference , the Jets have the fourth best average per passing attempt off play action in the league through the season’s first six weeks. However, only 22% of Jets passes come off play action per PFR, which is 21st highest in the league. What stands out to me is how often the Jets offense stalls on drives after a series of consecutive runs. This began in Week 1 when the Jets were forced to settle for a field goal after a 19 play drive. Against New England, the Jets had three first half drives stall out after a series four consecutive rushes. There has been a pattern of running effectively and then eventually getting stopped instead of building to deep shots off play action. I understand the argument that the Jets’ efficiency on play action might be aided by how infrequently they use it. It might catch opponents by surprise to a degree. Still, it’s notable to hear Glenn cite play action performance to defend his play caller, when there is some evidence that Reich isn’t leaning into it enough.

title: Eagles-Panthers Film Review: This defense needs help. It also needs to play better.
summary: Writing about the Eagles’ defense is becoming a slightly repetitive exercise. Once again, the offense made its job harder. Once again, the defense spent far too much time on the field. But even so, this defense isn’t playing well enough right now, and it certainly isn’t carrying this team. The workload is ridiculous. Just look… […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Cole Payton #18 attempts to complete a catch against Cooper DeJean #33 of the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Writing about the Eagles’ defense is becoming a slightly repetitive exercise. Once again, the offense made its job harder. Once again, the defense spent far too much time on the field. But even so, this defense isn’t playing well enough right now, and it certainly isn’t carrying this team. The workload is ridiculous. Just look… The Eagles played 79 snaps on defense against the Panthers. They have now played 70+ defensive snaps in 5 of 6 games this year. In 2025, they played 70+ defensive snaps in 6 of 17 games. In the 2024 Super Bowl season they played 70+ just 3 times all season. — Dave Zangaro (@DZangaroNBCS) October 19, 2026 That matters. It affects the rotation, the pass rush, and how much you can reasonably ask of players over four quarters. The offense has to give this group some help. However, the workload doesn’t explain everything we are seeing. There are communication problems in the secondary, missed tackles, and players who don’t look comfortable with their responsibilities. The Panthers deserve credit for finding those weaknesses and repeatedly attacking them. Imagine our staff did that? Let’s get into it. Defense The Panthers’ first play from 13 personnel set the tone in a few ways. The Eagles put Jihaad Campbell on the edge while keeping a split-safety structure behind the front. I’m not a huge fan of that combination here because it leaves Zack Baun as the lone off-ball linebacker with a lot of ground to cover. I think some of the Panthers’ success from 13 personnel opened up play action later on, too. As always, one thing that stands out when I watch other offenses is how well their tight ends block. Tommy Tremble had an excellent game, and his work here is part of what makes these heavier personnel packages useful. Having three tight ends on the field means very little if they cannot actually block anyone! Tremble looked like the sort of player the Eagles should be interested in if he becomes available. Based on this game, he would offer something they could use. To be fair, I doubt it’s hard to find tight ends that can block better than the Eagles’ current group. Eagles' Defense All22 Thread vs. Panthers. 1) I thought the first play of the game from 13 personnel set the tone in some ways. I'm not a huge fan of leaving Campbell at edge with a split-safety look because you end up asking Baun to cover a lot as the lone LB. As always, one… pic.twitter.com/QAej0RqXoL — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 20, 2026 The Panthers quickly identified a matchup they wanted: Tetairoa McMillan against Andrew Mukuba. They used motion to create it repeatedly in the first quarter, and Mukuba struggled to handle it. That is good offensive coaching. I didn’t see it much after the first quarter, so I’m guessing the Eagles made an adjustment, but not until they had 2 big completions. What frustrates me most about this particular play is how little else the secondary has to account for. The Panthers only send two receivers into routes, and the Eagles essentially have four defenders around McMillan. There should be enough help available to make this much harder. Instead, nobody gets in front of the route. Cooper DeJean needs communication from someone around him so he can get across and affect the throw. It just can’t be this easy. Something is missing in the secondary’s communication this year. These are the sorts of situations where you expect the coverage to squeeze the offense and take away an obvious threat. The Eagles aren’t doing that consistently, and I’m still not convinced by what we are seeing from DeJean at safety. Tariq Woolen cost the Eagles about $12 million on a one-year deal. He isn’t giving them value right now. 2) The Panthers used motion to get Tet McMillan on Andrew Mukuba repeatedly in the first quarter, and Mukuba couldn't handle it. Something just seems missing in the secondary's communication this year. The Eagles essentially have 4 players around McMillan with no other real… pic.twitter.com/04knuZfIYC — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 20, 2026 Here is the same idea again. The Panthers use motion into a switch release, which changes the receivers’ release paths and forces the secondary to sort out who is taking whom. Once again, McMillan ends up against Mukuba. Once again, the Panthers win. Mukuba has to perform better, but you also have to acknowledge how deliberately the Panthers created this matchup. They weren’t just lining up and hoping their best receiver would get open. They were using personnel, motion, and route distribution to get him against the defender they wanted. God, it is frustrating watching other offenses make things look this coherent. 3) Same idea, same result for the Panthers. The motion into a switch release gets McMillan on Mukuba, who can't handle it. God, it's frustrating to watch how well-designed other offenses are in the league. Sigh. pic.twitter.com/JoshC5TflR — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 20, 2026 There were good coverage snaps, too, and Campbell deserves credit for this one. His athleticism shows up as he gets across the field and takes away the crossing route. This is exactly the sort of movement ability that makes him worth developing. He can cover ground that many linebackers simply cannot. Nolan Smith ends up with the unblocked sack, and I know he seems to collect a fair few fortunate sacks. However, I don’t think it is entirely coincidence. Being athletic enough to close space and reliable enough to tackle a quarterback in the open field has value. Plenty of defenders get an opportunity like this and fail to finish it. Smith’s hustle and closing ability will create a few cleanup sacks every season, and there is nothing wrong with that. 4) Excellent coverage on this one, in particular by Jihaad Campbell, who shows his athleticism to get across and stop the crossing route, and Nolan Smith ends up with the unblocked sack. This is good coverage by Campbell here. Nolan Smith gets a hell of a lot of fortunate… pic.twitter.com/n9fuGeRzcb — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 20, 2026 There is plenty to like against the run here. Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter do their usual work up front, but I particularly wanted to highlight Jeremiah Trotter Jr. Watch how he avoids the center and gets to the ball carrier. He recognizes where he needs to go and gets there before the blocker can properly engage him. Keep that movement in mind because there is a useful comparison with Campbell later. Arnold Ebiketie also deserves some credit. He played 72 defensive snaps, a ridiculous workload for an edge defender, and he kept competing. Especially as he hasn’t played much this year, so there is no way his body would have been ready for this workload. I thought he fought hard throughout the game, and that will matter to the coaches. The Eagles needed a lot from him, and his effort deserves recognition. 5) A few excellent reps here vs. the run. JD and Carter do their usual stuff. I wanted to focus on how Trotter avoids the center to get to the ball carrier (to compare to Campbell later). This is something he does very well. I also wanted to mention Arnold Ebiketie. He had to… pic.twitter.com/JoDvR6CTRZ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 20, 2026 I know I can sound biased on this subject because I have never been particularly keen on moving DeJean to safety full-time. However, I’m not even convinced the current arrangement, with him playing safety in base and moving to nickel in other packages, is working. You can criticize Tariq Woolen for not getting enough depth here, but DeJean is also far too far away from Jalen Coker. Whatever the precise communication should be, the coverage cannot leave this much space around the…

title: Eagles News: Saquon Barkley included among 3 ESPN trade proposals
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles should absolutely trade Saquon Barkley if they get a good offer. Getting at least one second-round pick is probably key to making that deal work. A second-round pick and a third-round pick? Should be a no-brainer. Barkley is still […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 18: Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley (26) looks on after the game between the Carolina Panthers and Philadelphia Eagles on October 18, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles should absolutely trade Saquon Barkley if they get a good offer. Getting at least one second-round pick is probably key to making that deal work. A second-round pick and a third-round pick? Should be a no-brainer. Barkley is still good; it’s not a slam on him. Rather, it’s about him not really fitting the team’s timeline to contend moving forward. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 7: From Eagles to Matthew Stafford – ESPN RB Saquon Barkley to the Texans for a 2027 third-round pick, a 2027 sixth-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick and RB Woody Marks. Would the Eagles really trade Barkley? It feels bold, but if there’s a general manager willing to get out a year early instead of a year late on a 29-year-old running back, it’s certainly Roseman. When Roseman invested in Barkley in 2024 free agency, he was doing so with contention in mind — adding a final key piece to an offense that had a dominant offensive line and dominant wide receiver play. Now, in fall 2026, with a rebuild in mind, how likely is Barkley to remain a prime player the next time the Eagles are ready for playoff football? I waffle on this. Barkley could be a huge boon to a rookie-contract quarterback if they move on from Hurts. But the offensive line will need addressing first, as might wide receiver. I think the Eagles will say Barkley isn’t unavailable so that acquiring teams are compelled to send that can’t-refuse offer. Remember: Barkley, if traded, would hit the Eagles with about $26.5 million in dead cap in 2027 … on top of the $27.1 million Brown has already left behind. That’s a big hurdle to overcome. I could see a few contenders doing it. The Seahawks came to mind, as did the Packers and the Vikings. But I love the idea of GM Nick Caserio, fresh off the Marvin Harrison Jr. deal, doubling down on the offense and adding Barkley to a backfield that he has yet to solve in Houston. The Texans are once again on pace to have a bottom-5 rushing attack, but Barkley has the talent behind the line of scrimmage to help cover for a shaky interior offensive line group. By forcing opposing defenses to play more heavy boxes by formation and by the presence of Barkley, the 2-4 Texans could pull further defensive attention away from receiver Nico Collins and field an offense really worthy of a comeback run into the playoffs. Will the Eagles have a fire sale? Could they be buyers? A way-too-early look at the NFL trade deadline – Inquirer The Eagles have a few valuable trade candidates who aren’t on expiring deals, too. RB Saquon Barkley: This one doesn’t seem likely, but it’s worth considering. The two seasons following Barkley’s historic 2024 campaign haven’t gone as planned. The offensive line in front of him struggled in 2025. This year, Barkley has missed time with a hamstring injury. He’s signed for two more seasons, and the Eagles at least have the draft capital to not go full-blown rebuild mode. Why wouldn’t they want Barkley around for the next few seasons? Every player has a price, and while Barkley turns 30 in February, it’s not hard to imagine a team like Seattle or Minnesota parting with a premier draft pick to acquire him. It’s getting harder to see how the Eagles’ Jalen Hurts marriage ends well – BGN The simplest and cleanest way to get the Eagles back on track just may be to get rid of everyone, strip the coaching staff and the roster down, and retool. With a ton of draft picks, the Eagles could rebuild their lines and get a new QB pretty quickly. A new head coach/offensive coordinator would be able to identify the QB he believes would be best suited to run his offense and work on building a new program, starting in 2027. Unfortunately, that would mean Jalen Hurts is traded this off-season. Make no mistake, Hurts is the best quarterback in franchise history. It would be very interesting to see how things would work out if Sirianni was gone and an offensive-minded head coach was brought in who would tailor an offense around Hurts’ strengths. But it would also require Hurts to run the ball more often than he has, and if he’s decided he’s not a running QB anymore, then Hurts’ value as a franchise player decreases tremendously. Can Eagles defense hold up if it has to keep playing this much? – NBCSP The Eagles defense could be better. Let’s start off with that so this doesn’t read like an out-and-out excuse for that side of the football. Because this defense is supposed to be elite and it hasn’t been that yet this season. But the Eagles’ offense isn’t doing the defense any favors. In the 25-14 loss on Sunday at the Linc, the Eagles played 79 defensive snaps and saw 74 plays, while their offense was on the field for 64 snaps. The Eagles lost in time of possession 34:48-25:12. And this isn’t the first time we’ve seen the Eagles’ defense on the field this much. Because of that, it’s not surprising that unit keeps collapsing in the fourth quarter — 42% of the points the Eagles have given up have come in the fourth. Ultimately, it’s fair to wonder if the defense will be able to hold up at this rate. “Nobody is going to be perfect for that many plays and you’ve got to be able to deal with ups and downs each and every play,” Cooper DeJean said on Sunday evening. “The biggest thing is effort. Just putting in your best effort and communication and doing your job each and every play to the best of your ability.” Another Hurts Update – Iggles Blitz The Nick Sirianni press conference wasn’t ideal. The Eagles certainly could have handled that better. The right messaging can make situations like this so much less messy. Let’s hope they learn from this. I have no issue with the league doing an investigation. I have no problem with the media asking tough questions. This is a complex, bizarre story about the team’s star QB. I just hope people are better informed. The sleepless angle no longer exists. That is a real game-changer. We have a better idea of the timeline so everyone can understand how things went down. If new info emerges we’ll adjust the story and our conclusions. Hopefully this situation will settle down so we can get back to talking about the Eagles as a football team. Jalen Hurts’ recovery comes first. What’s next for his Eagles future? – The Athletic Earlier this year, owner Jeffrey Lurie was effusive in his support of Hurts, saying, “I love everything about him.” Lurie’s words spelled out support that the eventual lack of an offseason extension omitted. Hurts entered the third season of a five-year, $255 million extension. The deal’s guarantees decline significantly to $22 million after this season, according to Over the Cap. He has no guaranteed money left after 2027. Moving on still carries substantial salary-cap consequences, and Hurts’ no-trade clause gives him control over whether to approve a trade. The Eagles executed their biggest schematic shift in Sirianni’s tenure with Hurts still on the roster, which spoke to their collective confidence in the quarterback. But like Sirianni, first-time offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and the rest of the offensive staff, Hurts would be judged on his performance in the new offense. The first five weeks of the 2026 season suggested the Eagles’ offense would eventually require a full evaluation. The Eagles ranked 30th in the NFL in offensive EPA (-42.74), according to TruMedia. Their run game had the league’s ninth-lowest success rate (33.6 percent). Their play-action passes had the fourth-lowest EPA per dropback (-0.25) and the fifth-lowest yards per attempt…

title: Steelers’ Mike McCarthy named one of best new coaches
summary: After just over one-third in the NFL’s 2026 regular season, we’ve gotten a good look at the whopping 10 new head coaching hires across the league this year. And according to CBS Sports’ Garrett Podell, the Steelers’ hire of Mike McCarthy has been one of the best of the group. In a Tuesday piece grading […]
full_text: Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images | Getty Images After just over one-third in the NFL’s 2026 regular season, we’ve gotten a good look at the whopping 10 new head coaching hires across the league this year. And according to CBS Sports’ Garrett Podell, the Steelers’ hire of Mike McCarthy has been one of the best of the group. In a Tuesday piece grading and ranking every first-year head coach this season, Podell placed McCarthy in fourth place with a B- grade. “The Steelers are starting to find their groove under new head coach Mike McCarthy. Pittsburgh is averaging the fifth-most points per game (28.5) since Week 3, a major improvement after averaging the second-fewest points per game (11.5) in the league through the first two weeks,” Podell wrote . “Pittsburgh also just completed its largest fourth-quarter comeback (13 points, 16-3) since the 2002 AFC Wild Card Round against the Cleveland Browns in its 26-19 overtime road win at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. McCarthy’s offense has added more life this season to the Steelers’ attack, and Pittsburgh is in a 4-2 bottleneck at the top of the AFC North as a result.” With that aforementioned 4-2 record, McCarthy is currently in a three-way tie for the most wins among newly-hired head coaches, with the Bills’ Joe Brady (ranked second) leading the way at 5-1. Interestingly, despite McCarthy ranking high on the list, he’s still last among the three new head coaching hires in the AFC North this year, with the Browns’ Todd Monken (4-2, ranked first) and the Ravens’ Jesse Minter (4-2 record, ranked third) coming in slightly higher, per Podell’s list. Currently, the Steelers are ranked second in the division, but with three teams at 4-2 and the Bengals not far behind at 3-2, the AFC North is shaping up to be one of the NFL’s best and most competitive divisions this season. Despite being a new face in the division, McCarthy is still by far the most experienced head coach in the AFC North, with 18 prior seasons in the role during his time with the Packers and Cowboys. Over that span, he won his division eight times, and has yet to finish in last place. Now 62, it’s unclear how long McCarthy will coach the Steelers. During his time in Pittsburgh, he’ll be trying to make NFL history as the first head coach to win a Super Bowl with two separate teams.

title: Seahawks never offered Kenneth Walker a contract before free agency
summary: The Seattle Seahawks’ decision to let Kenneth Walker III leave in free agency has been one of the most debated moves of their offseason. With the former Super Bowl MVP thriving with the Kansas City Chiefs and Seattle struggling to establish a consistent running game, the conversation has often centered on the team’s decision to […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks’ decision to let Kenneth Walker III leave in free agency has been one of the most debated moves of their offseason. With the former Super Bowl MVP thriving with the Kansas City Chiefs and Seattle struggling to establish a consistent running game, the conversation has often centered on the team’s decision to retain Rashid Shaheed rather than bring Walker back. But according to a new report, that debate might have been built on the wrong premise: the Seahawks never even made Walker a contract offer. In a report for The Athletic , Mike Dugar revealed that Seattle did not engage in serious discussions about bringing Walker back before free agency. There were no serious discussions — on that day or any other — about Walker returning to the team that used a second-round draft pick on him in 2022. Walker’s postseason performance put him in such high demand that he effectively priced himself out of Seattle, which didn’t make a contract offer ahead of free agency, according to league sources not authorized to speak publicly about the matter. That revelation changes the context surrounding one of general manager John Schneider’s most scrutinized offseason decisions. Rather than a straightforward choice between paying Walker and investing in Shaheed, the report suggests Seattle never formally attempted to retain its starting running back. The Seahawks never made an offer to their Super Bowl MVP Walker’s departure was not entirely unexpected for the RB. The fourth-year running back had just completed a postseason run that transformed his standing around the league, finishing with 135 rushing yards in Seattle’s Super Bowl victory over the New England Patriots and earning MVP honors . His regular-season production was great, too. Walker rushed for 1,027 yards in 2025, although his role was shared with Zach Charbonnet, who scored 12 rushing touchdowns compared to Walker’s five. When Charbonnet suffered a torn ACL during the divisional-round win over the San Francisco 49ers, Walker became Seattle’s primary option and delivered 313 rushing yards and four touchdowns across the team’s final three playoff games. That performance helped establish his value heading into free agency. The Chiefs ultimately signed Walker to a three-year, $43 million contract, making him one of the highest-paid running backs in the NFL. Walker had already suggested that he knew his time in Seattle was coming to an end. Speaking to Mike Florio of Pro Football Talk in May, he explained that he had realized during the season that a return was unlikely. “Things ain’t work out how I was expecting it to, and that’s all right,” Walker said. “It worked out for the team. But yeah, (I knew) sometime during the season, and then we get to free agency, you pretty much know you weren’t going to be there.” The report also revisits the awkward moment during Seattle’s Super Bowl celebration when Schneider joked that Walker had tried negotiating a contract with him moments before taking the stage. Walker subsequently denied that account on Instagram, and Schneider later described the incident as a “panic moment.” As Dugar’s reporting now makes clear, there were no serious contract negotiations behind the joke. Kenneth Walker gets his chance to remind Seattle what it lost The timing of Dugar’s report could hardly be more significant. On Sunday, Walker will return to Lumen Field for the first time as an opponent when the Seahawks host the Chiefs on Sunday Night Football . His first season in Kansas City has been spectacular. Walker has rushed for 665 yards and six touchdowns in five games, leading the NFL in rushing yards at the time of Dugar’s report. He has also helped transform the Chiefs’ ground game into one of the league’s most productive units, giving Patrick Mahomes another way to punish defenses that focus too heavily on the passing attack. Seattle, meanwhile, has struggled to find that same balance. Its running backs have combined for 539 yards and three touchdowns, according to The Athletic , despite Walker producing more yardage individually while playing one fewer game. Injuries have contributed to the problem, including a chest issue that sent rookie Jadarian Price to injured reserve, but the contrast remains striking. The matchup will also present a major test for Seattle’s defense. The Seahawks have established themselves as one of the league’s strongest units against the run, and they will attempt to contain a player who knows the organization, its personnel and its home stadium intimately. Walker enters the game averaging 133 rushing yards per contest, making him a formidable challenge for a defense that has not allowed an opposing running back to reach 100 rushing yards since Week 8 of the 2024 season. For Walker, Sunday is an opportunity to demonstrate just how much his role has changed. In Seattle, he shared opportunities with Charbonnet and never received a contract offer that would have kept him with the franchise. In Kansas City, he has become a central piece of an offense built to maximize his explosive running ability. For the Seahawks, the reunion will bring renewed attention to a decision that looked increasingly questionable as the season progressed. That makes Sunday’s matchup more than a reunion with a former player. It is a chance for Walker to show Seattle what it is missing — and for the Seahawks to confront the consequences of an offseason decision that, according to the latest report, was made without even putting a contract offer on the table.
author: Alexandre Castro

title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from Seattle’s frustrating loss to Broncos
summary: The Seattle Seahawks offense was so dysfunctional that it managed to lose to a Denver Broncos offense that was barely more productive. Denver put together two touchdown drives and then practically disappeared, managing just 30 yards in the second half and eight more on its lone overtime possession. Yet the Seahawks couldn’t take advantage. Their […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks offense was so dysfunctional that it managed to lose to a Denver Broncos offense that was barely more productive. Denver put together two touchdown drives and then practically disappeared, managing just 30 yards in the second half and eight more on its lone overtime possession. Yet the Seahawks couldn’t take advantage. Their only touchdown came late in the fourth quarter, and even after rallying to force overtime, they couldn’t finish the job. Sam Darnold threw two interceptions, the offense struggled to sustain drives, and Seattle left crucial points on the field—including a missed Jason Myers field goal and a Rashid Shaheed fumble. The defense deserves credit for shutting Denver down after its two scoring drives, but the offensive mistakes proved too costly. At 3–3, with San Francisco already 6–0, Seattle has made its path through the NFC West and the playoff race considerably more difficult. The Bad 1. The defensive blackout on two drives Seattle’s defense is far from a bad unit this season, but it hasn’t consistently reached the level it showed last year. One concern has been its red-zone performance: opponents have too often turned scoring opportunities into touchdowns. That remains an issue worth monitoring, although the defense was not the main reason Seattle lost this game. The problem against Denver was a breakdown on two drives, both of which ended in touchdowns and accounted for all 14 of the Broncos’ points in regulation. Denver’s offense had been struggling, and its approach relied heavily on the running game and short passes, particularly screens to RJ Harvey. Still, Seattle allowed those two possessions to become the difference between winning and losing. The frustrating part is that the Seahawks had opportunities to end both drives. On a crucial fourth-and-three, Denver converted with a six-yard run by Tyler Badie. Seattle’s defensive alignment didn’t look well suited to defending the run: the interior gaps were open, and Byron Murphy was the only defensive tackle on the line, with Leonard Williams aligned as an edge defender. It’s unclear whether Seattle didn’t expect Denver to go for it, but the defense didn’t look fully prepared for the play. On the second touchdown drive, Seattle again had chances to get off the field. On third-and-ten, Byron Murphy’s facemask penalty gave Denver a fresh set of downs after an eight-yard completion. Later, a defensive pass-interference penalty on Devon Witherspoon helped put the Broncos in position to score from the one-yard line. Denver also found success with its screen game (nothing new), particularly when targeting Harvey on those two drives. Seattle looked overly aggressive and occasionally undisciplined in trying to shut those plays down. The defense seemed intent on attacking the ball carrier without consistently accounting for the space created by the offensive design. There were also several uncharacteristic missed tackles and poor angles—technical mistakes that are unusual for this defense. These weren’t simply two drives in which Denver executed brilliantly. Seattle had chances to make stops but let the Broncos off the hook through penalties, missed tackles and poor execution. The defense deserves criticism for those possessions, but context matters: after the touchdowns, Seattle adjusted and effectively shut Denver down. Two lapses proved costly, but they shouldn’t overshadow the defense’s response afterward. 2. Brian Fleury and the bad play calls Seattle’s offensive dysfunction can’t be blamed on one person. The quarterback, offensive line, running game and overall execution have all contributed. Still, Brian Fleury is part of the problem, and his play-calling is one of the areas where I have the least confidence in a major turnaround. There’s a difference between players failing to execute a good play and a coaching staff repeatedly putting them in difficult situations. Seattle has experienced both. Take the run-action concepts, for example. The offense continues to use designs intended to sell the threat of a run before creating a passing opportunity. These concepts can work when defenses respect the ground game, but Seattle hasn’t established a consistent rushing threat. Opponents aren’t particularly worried about the Seahawks’ running attack, which makes it harder to manipulate defenders with those looks. As a result, the offensive line is asked to execute complicated assignments without the benefit of a convincing rushing threat. Given how poorly the line has played, that increases the risk of communication errors, missed blocks and pressure reaching Darnold. The two-point conversion against Denver was another example of questionable play design. Darnold was put in motion toward one side of the field, effectively narrowing the space the defense had to defend. My read is that Cooper Kupp’s route was intended to create access for Jaxon Smith-Njigba, a concept Seattle has used successfully before. Denver covered both receivers, however, leaving Darnold with limited alternatives. The only other meaningful option was Rashid Shaheed, whose route developed from the opposite side. Darnold threw in his direction, and Shaheed made a good play to secure the catch. The conversion worked, but the design left very little margin for error once the primary options were covered. Third-down play-calling has also been a persistent issue. Too often, the route concepts look predictable, with straightforward vertical routes and few complementary options designed to create separation. The offense doesn’t consistently force defenders to cover different areas or choose between competing threats. One third-down play illustrates the problem. Smith-Njigba ran an option route that finished roughly six yards short of the line of scrimmage. Tory Horton’s route was near the first-down marker, while Kupp’s vertical route didn’t present much of a deep threat. The design didn’t appear to create an obvious advantage. Seattle converted because JSN is JSN: he escaped the initial tackle and gained the necessary yards after the catch. That’s a credit to the receiver, but it raises the question of whether the play design created the opportunity or whether Smith-Njigba simply rescued another uninspiring call. Spacing is another recurring concern. Good route spacing forces defenders to cover different areas and makes it harder to defend multiple options at once. When receivers converge on the same area, defenders can close passing lanes more efficiently and sometimes account for multiple threats with fewer players. Seattle has repeatedly shown this problem even when the play works. 3. Sam Darnold: The biggest problem on offense For me, Sam Darnold might be the biggest problem with this offense right now. He had another poor performance against Denver, throwing two interceptions and bringing his season total to seven. The most frustrating part is when those turnovers happen: both came at critical moments, and the overtime interception was particularly damaging. Seattle had fought its way back into the game, erased an 11-point deficit in the fourth quarter and forced overtime. The defense then gave the offense an opportunity to win. Instead, Darnold threw an interception that gave Denver the ball at Seattle’s 43-yard line. The Broncos didn’t need a first down to set up Wil Lutz’s game-winning field goal. Darnold has been inconsistent in his decision-making, playing too conservatively when he should take an opportunity and too aggressively when he should protect the ball. On one play, JSN was open downfield, but Darnold needed to hold the ball a little longer. Perhaps he was reluctant to take a hit behind an offensive line he doesn’t trust. title: Seahawks Week 7 power rankings: Seattle drops again after another turnover-filled loss
summary: Entering Week 6, the Seattle Seahawks slid back down the power rankings after losing to the San Francisco 49ers. After losing their second game in a row to the Denver Broncos, how much farther will they fall? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Sam Darnold #14 of the Seattle Seahawks looks on prior to the game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Andrew Wevers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Entering Week 6, the Seattle Seahawks slid back down the power rankings after losing to the San Francisco 49ers . After losing their second game in a row to the Denver Broncos, how much farther will they fall? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. Let’s start with the worst news. NFL.com dropped the Seahawks down three spots to 10th best in the NFL . In their ranking, they mention Sam Darnold’s “turnover problem.” However, they also remain optimistic that the offense as a whole can turn it around with the offensive line returning to full strength soon. B/R also dropped Seattle down three spots, from 6th to 9th . B/R also remains optimistic about the team considering their running back room is returning to health. However, they also mention the turnover issues as a big issue the team needs to address moving forward. Both CBS and PFT have the Seahawks ranked as 7th best in the league. PFT who moved the team down two spots simply state “[t]hey should’ve kept Kenneth Walker III .” CBS meanwhile didn’t move Seattle at all, and kept them ranked at number 7. In their ranking, CBS also highlighted that “Sam Darnold is turning the ball over way too much. ” The highest ranking the Seahawks got from a national site this week was from ESPN, who ranked Seattle as the 6th best team in the NFL . Despite this higher ranking, ESPN also talked about the turnover issues. ESPN notes that the Seahawks have committed 12 turnovers, third most of any offense so far. Ten of those turnovers came in Seattle’s three losses. Overall, it would be surprising if the Seahawks did not drop down in the national power rankings. Losing two games in a span of five days will do that. Turnovers were the clear trend in all of these rankings. However, despite these woes the Seahawks are still firmly in the top ten of the NFL. Entering Week 6, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 5.0. Entering week 7, that average has fallen to 7.8. The Seahawks face Kenneth Walker III and the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs next week on Sunday Night Football. Will Seattle be able to bounce back or will the slide down continue into week 8.

title: 49ers News: We’re on to Atlanta
summary: My bad on missing yesterday’s nuggets. Even Christian McCaffrey fumbles sometimes.  Atlanta is always a tough out, no matter how bad they are. They can just bizarrely win against the 49ers for whatever reason. Their defense is looking good. I read an interesting article on the Athletic about it… their d-line coach, this guy named […]
full_text: SAN FRANCISCO, CA - DECEMBER 23: Inside linebacker NaVorro Bowman #53 of the San Francisco 49ers returns an interception for a touchdown in the fourth quarter against the Atlanta Falcons during a game at Candlestick Park on December 23, 2013 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Stephen Dunn/Getty Images) | Getty Images My bad on missing yesterday’s nuggets. Even Christian McCaffrey fumbles sometimes. Atlanta is always a tough out, no matter how bad they are. They can just bizarrely win against the 49ers for whatever reason. Their defense is looking good. I read an interesting article on the Athletic about it… their d-line coach, this guy named Nate Ollie, does a Kris Kocurek / peak Saleh days impersonation with his “attack-style defense”. He tells his players that if “they think, they stink”, so the defensive linemen have to do nothing but go after the ball. It’s lead to their interior defenders leading the league, with Brandon Dorlus tied for #1 most QB pressures from an interior d-lineman. Their back seven is asked to do more, and while Divine Deablo is one of the better linebackers (and best names) in the league, there’ll often be space to be found if the 49ers linemen get to the second level effectively enough. It’ll be fascinating to see how Kyle Shanahan attacks that without anybody at wide receiver. The end of last game has my antennas up a little bit, but I’m still confident in my preseason prediction. No Nick Bosa for the 49ers; Kyle Shanahan is hopeful he returns on Thursday “Since the 49ers played on Monday, Shanahan said Wednesday’s practice will be a walkthrough. Linebacker Dre Greenlaw returns to practice. As for wide receiver Christian Kirk, Shanahan said, “He had a good week of practice last week. He’ll be out there again today. Hopefully, he feels good at the end of the week.” Kyle Shanahan shares updates ahead of 49ers-Falcons game “It’s actually not call the play faster. It’s, ‘I need it again.’ It gets cut off at 15, so sometimes no one can hear and a lot of the quarterbacks do it because I always call a play and then I just walk and think. I don’t always watch the huddle and a lot of times [QB] Mac [Jones] or someone, because they’ll be like, ‘Hey, we didn’t get it. It was choppy.’ Or someone will yell, ‘Brock’s yelling at you,’ which I can’t always hear. I did hear him a couple of times in this game, so I look up and then I try to do it again as long as it’s not past 15 seconds. Sometimes he’ll do it and I don’t get a heads up to like 16 and I start to do it again and he hears half the play call because it shuts off at 15…..I don’t remember what the play was. Probably happened five times in the game, so that’s something that happens a lot. Headsets do that.” Nick Bosa misses practice Wednesday, but 49ers hope he will return this week “(He) can’t go today but hoping he’ll be out there tomorrow,” Shanahan said of Bosa. 49ers minutia minute: Rookies Romello Height, Jaden Dugger shined on defense (paywall) “ In the run-up to the game, Halton talked about “building a cage” against the elusive Daniels, who ran for 103 yards and two touchdowns a week earlier, then followed through by snagging Daniels for a sack as he tried to escape in the second quarter. Fred Warner was blitzing on the play, and Daniels would have had room to roam had Halton not taken him down. The 49ers hit Daniels a season-high 10 times. To put that in perspective, they sacked Sam Darnold five times last week but finished with eight quarterback hits. Raheem Morris is back in Atlanta — and he’s bringing his surging 49ers defense “Morris is also utilizing more “match” coverage, which asks defenders to start in traditional zone drops, keep their eyes on the quarterback and read routes to tighten up throwing lanes. If a pass catcher crosses into their path, the defender picks up that player, often only turning him loose for checkdowns and short gains. The approach has not only served to limit big plays, but it has also allowed the secondary to be more active. That was evident in Green’s two-interception game in Seattle and Mustapha’s jarring hits to help seal Monday night’s win over Washington. “Those guys aren’t counting on linebackers, so they have to be more aggressive in coverage,” Shanahan said. “Those guys are playing concepts to stop plays without any help and that’s been their edge. I think it’s made them better. It’s given them more confidence in practice, and I think that’s what we’re all seeing in games.” How long might 49ers’ Mike Evans be sidelined? Surgeon provides perspective on Achilles tendinitis (paywall) “Achilles tendinitis is an overuse injury, an inflammation of the tendon, that causes pain and tightness. Serious cases can involve microscopic degeneration, small tears in the fibers in the middle of the tendon, that can increase the odds of a rupture. Given Evans’ age, and history with Achilles tendinitis, Jung said Evans is likely dealing with “wear and tear,” minor tissue degeneration that might have progressed to the point where he has had a flare-up severe enough to sideline him. Evans did not miss a game due to an Achilles issue in his first 12 seasons. Achilles tendinitis is often treated with rest, icing and supportive footwear. Many cases can resolve within a few weeks. Assuming Evans didn’t seriously exacerbate his condition by playing Monday, it’s conceivable he could miss just one game….“If it’s just some (Achilles) wear and tear, then you’re probably in a situation where you’re managing it,” Jung said. “You try to get it to a point where it settles down, it doesn’t flare up and you just kind of keep managing it.”

title: 5 final observations from 49ers win over Commanders: A new part of the offense is starting to blossom
summary: The San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders 23-17 in Week 6, improving to 6-0 in a game where they nearly blew a 20-point lead in the second half. The injury bug continued for the 49ers, with Mike Evans missing the second half due to Achilles tendonitis, which coincided with San Francisco putting up just […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Washington Commanders during the third quarter of the game at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders 23-17 in Week 6, improving to 6-0 in a game where they nearly blew a 20-point lead in the second half. The injury bug continued for the 49ers, with Mike Evans missing the second half due to Achilles tendonitis, which coincided with San Francisco putting up just three points over the final 30 minutes, while going three-and-out on their final three drives. There was still plenty to like from the win, and a couple of trends that are playing out for the 49ers on their hot start to the season. Here are five final observations from the Niners win on Monday night. Niners run game is coming along A lot of talk came on the passing game, especially given the efficiency that Brock Purdy had when Mike Evans was on the first in the first half. San Francisco ended up scoring three touchdowns on five drives in the first half, holding a 20-3 lead at halftime. But it wasn’t just their pass game that connected. The 49ers run game is really starting to come along over the last two weeks. San Francisco had the highest EPA per rush by a wide margin in the NFL in Week 6. Their rushing success rate was 66.7 percent, easily the best by over 16 percent to the next-best team as well. With the injuries in the pass game, the 49ers gave Christian McCaffrey 25 total touches (16 rushes, nine targets), as he went for 117 yards from scrimmage with two touchdowns. While his 4.0 yards per carry number may not pop off on the box score, from an efficiency perspective, San Francisco had a great day on the ground. What’s even more impressive is that it came against the No. 8 defense in EPA allowed per rush coming into Monday. A week ago, McCaffrey ran for 68 yards on 11 carries against Seattle’s elite defense. Now, they had another pretty good game on the ground, which is coming at a good time with the Niners issues at wide receiver. OL might be 2nd MVP Brock Purdy is a serious MVP contender for a good reason; he’s been playing at an extremely high level all year long with his decision making, and the quarterback had another good game on Monday. But the offensive line, which has caught a lot of flak over the years, has really done its part this season. The 49ers have been quite good in pass protection this season, as Purdy wasn’t sacked over the first four weeks of the year. He’s taken five the last two weeks, but I would argue the two on Monday weren’t against the offensive line. In addition, we’re finally seeing the run game come to fruition the last two weeks, and the blocking there has started to come together. Trent Williams is playing at high level. Dominick Puni has had a good season outside of a rough Week 6. The group as a whole is clicking, and you’re seeing the continuity and experience be key factors as well. Mike Evans certainly has a case to be the offense’s other MVP, but the offensive line has done its part this season. Raheem Morris’s pressure plan is working Monday’s game was one where I had to tip my cap to Jayden Daniels. He had a great game, throwing for 300 yards while completing over 72 percent of his passes. It was not a good day for the 49ers cornerbacks overall, but Daniels has been a dangerous quarterback whenever healthy, and he was that on Monday as well. That’s why it’s impressive the 49ers were able to hold Washington to just three points at halftime and 17 for the whole game. Normally, when a quarterback is clicking like Daniels was on Monday, the pass rush isn’t consistently getting there. But the 49ers pressured Daniels on 21 of his 47 dropbacks on Monday and got five sacks, despite still being without Nick Bosa. It was a really good day for the young Niners defensive linemen. As I mentioned in the takeaways, Keion White, Romello Height, Gracen Halton, Sebastian Valdez, and Mykel Williams made plays, while Osa Odighizuwa added five pressures and a sack as well. Even on a rough day for his secondary and Jayden Daniels consistently getting the ball out quickly, Raheem Morris deliered with another good pressure plan against a fairly solid offensive line. Pass rate over expected Interestingly, despite the 49ers lead and injuries at wide receiver, Brock Purdy had a 14 percent pass rate over expected (69.6 percent vs. 55.5 percent) in “non-garbage time” situations. With how the 49ers were running the ball from a success rate and efficiency standpoint, I thought that number would end up being lower, but the 49ers were throwing the ball at a very efficient rate in the first half. On the season, that number has just been 3.5 percent over expected. So, it was interesting to see such a spike for Week 6. In those situations, the 49ers threw the ball 62.5 percent of the time on 1st down (5 of 8). We’ll see what trends change in Week 7 if the 49ers are to be without Mike Evans, but that was one number that caught my eye when looking back at Monday’s game. WR room shaking out To me, a win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7 feels like a luxury right now. San Francisco will be facing an elite rush defense, and I’m not expecting Mike Evans in right now after sitting out the second half on Monday. I haven’t been an advocate for the 49ers trading for a receiver, and I think that stance still stands heading closer to the trade deadline. While Evans will have to battle through the Achilles tendonitis for the rest of the season, he should be a go following the bye week. The 49ers are getting Christian Kirk back as well soon, and Deebo Samuel and Demarcus Robinson could be other candidates to return after the bye. There’s also De’Zhaun Stribling, who could return around Week 12 or so according to his timeline. So, the 49ers are certainly banged up right now at wide receiver, but I don’t know that they’ll make a move for one considering the depth they have returning from injury. Now, we did learn a bit about the 49ers receiver room this week. Jordan Watkins got the start, and Jacob Cowing’s role continued to diminish (he had a bad return decision as well). Watkins played 47 snaps, while Cooks played 32 snaps. Cowing could factor in again here in Week 8 with the banged-up room, but he might be the one inactive when all the injured wideouts return.

title: How the Falcons’ defense will attack the 49ers on Sunday
summary: The San Francisco 49ers will travel to Atlanta to face the Falcons and try to keep their unbeaten streak alive. Monday night’s victory over Washington was hard-fought, especially after Mike Evans left the game with an Achilles injury. Still, the 49ers held off the Commanders’ comeback attempt and moved to 6-0. The question becomes which […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers will travel to Atlanta to face the Falcons and try to keep their unbeaten streak alive. Monday night’s victory over Washington was hard-fought, especially after Mike Evans left the game with an Achilles injury. Still, the 49ers held off the Commanders’ comeback attempt and moved to 6-0. The question becomes which receivers will be available for Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy, and how the game plan must change without Evans on Sunday. Now, Evans isn’t ruled out, but as of now, it seems wise to hold him out until after the bye week. As easy as that sounds, it still leaves the 49ers with potentially Brandin Cooks, Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing, and potentially Christian Kirk, in some capacity. Yeah, I didn’t like typing that as much as you didn’t like reading it. Did Washington leave some breadcrumbs for Atlanta defensively on Monday night after Evans departed? I believe the Commanders did tip Atlanta’s hand a bit as to their potential strategy in the second half of Monday night’s game. Coming into the game, the Commanders were second in the NFL in blitz rate. The first half saw modest blitz numbers as Brock Purdy and Mike Evans marched up and down the field. Once Evans left, the Commanders spammed blitz after blitz in the second half, raising the first-half percentage from the 20s to the 70s. Washington wanted to speed up Purdy, and without separators or receivers that he trusts, the offense stalled. To be fair, I don’t blame Purdy at all for the second half. When you have receivers running into each other and not getting proper spacing and timing (I’m looking at you, Cooks and Watkins), Purdy can’t hit anticipatory throws to receivers he doesn’t trust. So, what will Atlanta do with Jeff Ulbrich as the defensive coordinator? In years past, especially last year, Atlanta has been at the top of the league in blitz rate. This year has seen the blitz rate go in the opposite direction. The Falcons are 25th in the NFL with a blitz rate of 25.9%. You can expect a total increase, as the Falcons sit in cover 3 38.3% of the time, and allowing Purdy time in the pocket allows him to pick apart zone coverages. You can expect an increase in the one coverage concept that is man coverage in Cover 1 (21.1%). Until the 49ers prove they have receivers available that secondaries should worry about, the blitzing will continue. If the receiver group can prove they can separate and be on proper timing, it will put the Falcons on their heels and the scales tip towards the 49ers. The chess match between Ulbrich and Shanahan will be fascinating. Shanahan will have to craft a game plan around running the football, screens, and quick throws until opportunities present themselves to attack downfield. The good news is this is a one-week issue, as after the bye, the 49ers can expect Evans, Demarcus Robinson, and Deebo Samuel to return to action. Sunday’s game presents an interesting challenge for Shanahan, and this is a game where his game plan and scheme should do the heavy lifting.
