title: NFL Week 7 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we're hearing
summary: Will the Seahawks stick with Sam Darnold past this season? Could Vita Vea get trade interest? What's next for the NFC East teams? And could the Colts make more changes?
full_text:
Week 7 of the  2026 NFL season  has arrived. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 What does the future hold for Bo Nix , Jalen Hurts , C.J. Stroud and other quarterbacks with looming contract situations? Who are some players who might be flying under the radar as trade candidates ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline? Will the Colts -- who just fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday -- keep making changes as they try to right the ship? And which of the NFC East teams in flux are most likely to shake things up in the coming weeks?

 It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 7.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 QB situations | Colts' next moves 
 Sneaky trade candidates 
 NFC East shake-ups |  Fantasy advice 
 More notes, intel 

 
 

 What is the most intriguing quarterback contract situation for the offseason? 
 Graziano: I recognize that there are far more important real-life situations going on around this player right now, but for me, it's the Eagles' Jalen Hurts . He is signed through 2028, but the only guaranteed money left on his contract after this season will be $22 million of his $51.5 million salary in 2027. Regardless of how this season was to play out for Hurts and the Eagles, there was always going to be an offseason discussion about whether to extend him again -- and if so, at what level -- or look into other options.

 The Eagles have some young stars coming up for extensions pretty soon, including cornerbacks Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean , and carrying a huge quarterback salary beyond this year is going to get more difficult. It's fair to wonder what impact Hurts being out for the rest of the season will have on the Eagles' decision-making.

 Fowler: Hurts belongs high on the list, as it's worth wondering whether he has played his last down as an Eagle. He is 59-28 as a starter for the franchise, but Philadelphia, which is often proactive with contracts of core players, did not extend Hurts last offseason. So, it's difficult to pinpoint where things will stand three to four months from now.

 But my pick is the Broncos' Bo Nix . Denver is good enough to keep winning despite Nix showing a limited ceiling. He is a quality starter but is not poised to enter the upper echelon. Confidence appears to be an issue this season, raising questions about what this player-team marriage looks like long term.

 To be sure, the conditions around Nix aren't perfect . Denver is struggling to run the ball and effectively create explosive plays off play-action. He has had two playcallers this season. Nix got skewered for last week's performance versus Seattle . But Denver didn't have as big of a problem with it because it had to play conservatively in a tight game between two great defenses, as whichever team won the turnover battle was probably going to win the game. Broncos coach Sean Payton knew that and most certainly relayed it to Nix, whose struggles against the 49ers in Week 4 were considered more problematic. That said, Nix -- who broke his right ankle in January -- doesn't appear to be the runner he once was. His viability with Denver might hinge on how he plays over the next 11 or so games.

 

 Graziano: I did have someone last week tell me the big difference with Nix was that he's not getting himself out of bad spots with his legs the way he did last season but that he doesn't look much different otherwise. But that lack of running is a big deal, and if it doesn't improve, we could be left watching his flaws the rest of the way.

 I'm a bit curious about  Sam Darnold 's situation, as he'll have one year left on his contract after this season. He is scheduled to make $35.5 million in 2027, but none of that money is guaranteed. There is a $10 million roster bonus that vests on the fifth day of the league year (March 16), so the Seahawks will want to decide by then whether they want him on next year's team. But if they do, they'd also look to extend him beyond that.

 What's interesting to me is that this is a different setup than Darnold had last offseason, when $17.5 million of his 2026 compensation became guaranteed on the fifth day after the Super Bowl. That was a no-brainer, of course, since Seattle  won the Super Bowl with him five days earlier. But if this season doesn't go as well (the Seahawks are 3-3, and only Justin Herbert has thrown more interceptions than Darnold's seven), Seattle has four more weeks to make the decision on Darnold than it did a year ago.

 Fowler: It's not helping that Drew Lock has been impressive for the Seahawks, both behind the scenes and in relief of Darnold. Darnold has earned a lot of street cred with Seattle, but he must limit the turnovers, especially with the team's dominant defense.

 Houston's C.J. Stroud is fueling the offseason intrigue with his excellent play. He is putting up MVP-type numbers, pacing for nearly 4,900 passing yards over a 17-game slate while registering only one interception on 219 passing attempts. Betting on himself in Year 4 should literally pay off. The Texans were willing to extend Stroud on a deal worth well above $50 million per year. But Stroud saw a bigger picture: a growing quarterback market and his place in it. Stroud and Carolina's Bryce Young both appear well-positioned for offseason negotiations. And Houston's trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.  -- Stroud's teammate while at Ohio State -- amplifies the Texans' feelings on Stroud.

 

 
 What's next for the Colts? Could more moves be coming? 
 Fowler: It feels as if  everything is on the table in Indianapolis, from an eventual head coaching change to a quarterback demotion, barring an uptick in performance. Daniel Jones ' play -- 30th in QBR (38.2) with 1.5 turnovers per game -- is unsustainable over a 17-game season. This situation mirrors that of the 2025 Dolphins, who fired general manager Chris Grier in October but evaluated coach Mike McDaniel over the remainder of the season, only to fire him four days after Week 18 . Miami also benched a quarterback with a high-priced contract  in  Tua Tagovailoa  late in the campaign.

 The sentiment as of now is that Colts coach Shane Steichen will get more chances to state his case for the job moving forward. But typically, franchises like to synchronize their brain trust on similar timelines, often with a newly appointed general manager spearheading a search for the new coach. That might not bode well for Steichen, whose acumen never has been questioned. He'd be in the mix for head coaching jobs or primo playcaller positions in the 2027 cycle. I'm curious about your take, Dan, but I believe team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon plans to place her stamp on the franchise in a big way over the coming months.

 

 Graziano: I would agree that while Steichen is well-regarded and well-liked in the building, this is definitely a situation worth monitoring for potential change at the end of the season, if not sooner. Firing a GM in mid-October  indicates disappointment from ownership, obviously, but it also signals the possibility of major change on the roster, maybe even in the next few weeks. The NFL trade deadline is Nov. 10 -- less than three weeks from now -- and the Colts have a very interesting roster. There were a number of veterans who could have received contract extensions this past offseason, and the only one who got one was running back Jonathan Taylor .

 High-profile veteran players such as offensive lineman Quenton Nelson , defensive linemen DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart , and wide receivers Josh Downs and Keenan Allen are on contracts that expire at the end of the season. If the Colts (who are without a 2027 first-round pick as a result of last year's Sauce Gardner trade ) want to try to regain some draft capital, they could look to deal some players who they don't view as part of…

title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why this is the week to use Texans, Jets
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and ranking the top five options for Week 7.
full_text:
In a season full of big upsets, Week 6 featured the most carnage all season. 58% of the remaining ESPN Survivor entries were eliminated, leaving just 4% of the original 1.2 million entries still alive.

 Last week's loss by the Los Angeles Rams against the Arizona Cardinals knocked out 35% of Survivor entries. Sadly, that also included this column's entry. The Rams became the first double-digit favorite to lose all season. The most popular Survivor pick has now lost in four of the first six weeks.

 But that wasn't the only major upset. The Tennessee Titans got their first win of the year, overcoming a 13-0 deficit to upset the Indianapolis Colts , knocking out another 16% of entries. The only top-three favorite to win were the New England Patriots , who handled the New York Jets at home.

 

 For those of you who survived, congratulations, but now you are facing one of the most difficult decisions of the season. The only team favored by more than a touchdown is the Houston Texans , hosting the New York Giants . Shockingly, ESPN's current selection on Houston as of Wednesday morning is just 12%, but I assume that number will grow significantly by Sunday. They will almost certainly be the chalk on Circa and Splash.

 Every other team has major question marks. The Denver Broncos and San Francisco 49ers both face lesser opponents, but both are on the road, and do you really want to use the 49ers here if you still have them? Do you trust the Minnesota Vikings offense? Do you trust the Jets or Dallas Cowboys at all? How do you handle the Rams after last week's debacle in Arizona?

 On ESPN, it's hard to get off the Texans as the top pick as of Wednesday morning based on the early-week selection numbers. However, if the Texans numbers rise as expected, they are by no means a must-play, with the Vikings and Jets both strong picks. If you are looking for a sub-10% play, one option is the Pittsburgh Steelers , who took sharp money early in the week against the Saints and allow you to burn a below-average team with reasonable win equity.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. Houston Texans (vs. Giants) 

 

 As is often the case with the biggest favorite of the week, the biggest questions are selection rate and future value. On ESPN, the Texans are only 12% selected as of Wednesday morning, but I expect them to be over 20% in most groups with a chance of reaching over 30%. Keep an eye on your individual group's availability for Houston. The Texans are 77% available overall on ESPN, but that number is likely lower in competitive groups, which could help suppress their selection a bit.

 Houston has an interesting schedule down the road where outside of Week 18 against the Titans, most of their easiest games come on the road (Week 9 at Los Angeles Chargers , Week 10 at Cleveland Browns , Week 11 vs. Indianapolis Colts , Week 14 at Washington Commanders , Week 16 at Philadelphia Eagles ). None of those are must-play spots, but given the Texans' rising team quality and the possibility for those teams imploding, they could have more value down the road than meets the eye.

 
 Chance to win: 84% (ESPN Analytics), 71% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Texans -10 (-520 moneyline) 
 Future value: 12th 
 Availability: 77% 
 ESPN Selection: 12% 
 
 2. New York Jets (vs. Dolphins) 
 

 This is the biggest test yet of the fade-the-Dolphins theory. The Jets are a bottom-10 team, and the only other week they'll be in Survivor consideration is Week 12 in Miami. Given that, I like the Jets more in double-pick pools, as you get to maintain the most flexibility going forward while giving up very little in immediate win equity. As scary as it is to rely on the Jets with so much of the pool already eliminated, the Jets dominated the Tennessee Titans in Week 1 and beat the Browns in Week 5, so they have played well against teams at or below their weight class this season. Plus, the defense has been dominant against the worst offenses on its schedule.

 
 Chance to win: 66% (ESPN Analytics), 82% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Jets -4.5 (-230 moneyline) 
 Future value: 24th 
 Availability: 98% 
 ESPN Selection: 11% 
 

 3. Minnesota Vikings (vs. Colts) 

 The Vikings are also a strong pick this week. Similar to Houston, they have already been used by a significant percentage of the field. Their future value is limited after this week, though home games against the Commanders (Week 16), Atlanta Falcons (Week 12) and Carolina Panthers (Week 13) could look better down the road. They also visit the Jets in Week 17.

 

 The Vikings are the second-biggest favorites in the betting market, though our two models have major disagreement. They are the biggest favorites of the week according to Mike Clay's model, though ESPN Analytics is way lower. Ultimately, given the Texans are significantly bigger favorites in the betting market, while our two models see very little difference between the Jets and Vikings, I break the tie slightly towards the Jets as the No. 2 pick.

 
 Chance to win: 65% (ESPN Analytics), 84% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Vikings -6.5 (-278 moneyline) 
 Future value: 16th 
 Availability: 58% 
 ESPN Selection: 12% 
 

 4. Pittsburgh Steelers (vs. Saints) 
 

 The Steelers are the contrarian pick of the week, particularly if you have already used the Texans and Vikings. They have minimal future value, especially on Splash, where their only two remaining games with a win probability over 60% are Week 8 (vs. Browns) and Week 11 (at Eagles). They took sharp money early in the week to move the line from 2.5 to 3.5.

 However, while I expect the three teams above them on this list to take up at least half of the remaining entries, the Steelers will likely remain less than 5% selected. If your path to make it to Week 7 involved a lot of chalk picks and the best teams in the NFL, pivoting to Pittsburgh could be a way to start to differentiate your entry.

 
 Chance to win: 60% (ESPN Analytics), 81% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Steelers -3.5 (-180 moneyline) 
 Future value: 19th 
 Availability: 85% 
 ESPN Selection: 3% 
 

 5. Dallas Cowboys (at Eagles) 
 If you just look at win equity, team quality and projected selection, the Cowboys are underrated at fifth in these rankings. Much of the public will be scared off of them after laying eggs against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Green Bay Packers in primetime in each of the past two weeks.

 However, as bad as the Cowboys have looked, they actually are a strong option in three of the next five weeks after this one. They host the Cardinals next week, the Titans in Week 11 and get a home rematch against the Eagles in Week 12. As banged up as the Eagles are, they still had a chance to win each of the last three weeks in the fourth quarter, and with this game being a division rivalry in Philadelphia, that's enough to prevent me from making the Cowboys a priority.

 
 Chance to win: 69% (ESPN Analytics), 65% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Cowboys -4.5 (-218 moneyline) 
 Future value: 14th 
 Availability: 96% 
 ESPN Selection: 4%

title: Cowboys' season looks bleak but schedule offers some hope
summary: Cowboys players and coaches are focused on a stretch of games versus teams that are struggling just like them.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- Quarterback  Dak Prescott has been around long enough to know the general feeling around the Dallas Cowboys at the moment.

 No one inside the organization -- ownership, personnel, coaches and players -- expected the team would be 2-4 after six games when they left Oxnard, California, at the end of training camp. They didn't expect the defense to be as porous as last year's, and certainly none of them expected the offense that returned nearly everybody from 2025 to be as inconsistent as it has been through six games.

 "When your guys believe, you've got a chance," Prescott said following Sunday's 23-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers . "And we know right now that we're probably the only ones, the guys in the locker room are the only ones who do believe."

 The rough start has led to the typical reactionary takes from fans: owner and general manager Jerry Jones needs to hire a real general manager; coach Brian Schottenheimer is over his head; the effort is lacking. The fans could be put off by the 31-year Super Bowl drought, or it could be recent failures.

 

 The Cowboys had three straight 12-5 finishes from 2021 to 2023 but that seems a long time ago. It is as if the organization has not recovered from the 48-32 loss to the Packers in the wild-card round of the 2023 playoffs when a team that went undefeated at AT&T Stadium in the regular season was bludgeoned at home in the postseason.

 Since then, the Cowboys are 16-23-1. While a good amount of the roster has been changed over -- only seven starters remain -- the success has disappeared.

 Yet there is an opportunity for the Cowboys to get others to believe again, at least temporarily.

 Five of the Cowboys' next six games, beginning with Monday's matchup against the similarly disappointing and 2-4 Philadelphia Eagles  ( 8:15 p.m. ET, ABC/ESPN ), are against teams with a combined 9-21 record. Only the San Francisco 49ers , who come to AT&T Stadium on Nov. 15, have a winning record (6-0).

 The Cowboys play Philadelphia twice in that span, the second meeting coming on Thanksgiving. The Eagles have been hurt by retirements and decimated by injury, including quarterback  Jalen Hurts  being ruled out Monday for the remainder of the season due to blood clots in his lungs .

 The Arizona Cardinals (Nov. 1) are 2-4 and coming off an upset win against the disappointing 2-4 Los Angeles Rams . The Cardinals have beaten the Cowboys four straight times but are hardly a vexing opponent. The Indianapolis Colts (Nov. 8) fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday. The Tennessee Titans (Nov. 22) are 1-5 and coming off their first win of the season.

 But it's not about the Eagles, Cardinals, Colts or Titans. Nor is it about the 49ers.

 "It's what's going on right here," cornerback DaRon Bland said. "I can't think about everything on the outside. I've got to think about what's right here and what we got in the room."

 

 Last week, the Cowboys added Mike Pettine as a senior defensive assistant  to aid first-time coordinator Christian Parker. Against the Packers, the Cowboys' defense had its first interception of the season, held Green Bay's run game in check (though it ranks even lower than the Cowboys) and had its first three-sack game of the season -- though the team allowed 11 third-down conversions and seven pass plays of 15 yards or more.

 The perplexing development has been the implosion of the offense with only 29 combined points over the past two games.

 Schottenheimer said, "We have great trust in our offense." He added that the poor execution falls on the players and the coaches.

 "I'm always honest with these guys. I raise my voice a lot with these guys," Schottenheimer said. "But again, how you get the message across to me is more about being upfront and honest and direct. And that's the way we talk, whether we win or we lose. And I think it's your responsibility as a head coach to paint the picture of why you either won or you lost."

 Whether it's a paint-by-numbers or some sort of Picasso, the Cowboys hope the picture can change quickly.

 "The answer is to win," left guard Tyler Smith said. "When you're losing, the only way you get out of a wreck like this is to win. And ultimately, I think winning just starts with being consistent with how you prepare. Ultimately, correcting the mistakes that you made.

 "I feel like we're not playing our best ball right now. I don't think we're anywhere [near] where we could be. I just feel like we just need to find a little bit more consistency with the way we play."

title: Lions to get DB Brian Branch, C Cade Mays back vs. Packers
summary: The Lions will have both Branch and center Cade Mays for Sunday's game against the Green Bay Packers.
full_text:
DETROIT -- Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell was growing tired of hearing his star defensive back  Brian Branch plead his case for when he should return to the field. After a 10-month absence, Branch is finally in position to receive his wish this week.

 As the Lions prepare to host the Green Bay Packers in their first NFC North battle of the 2026 season, both Branch and center Cade Mays are expected to suit up.

 "Barring anything negatively happening between now and the game, we plan on playing both of those guys," Campbell said of Branch and Mays on Monday.

 

 The Lions officially opened the 21-day practice windows for Branch (Achilles) and Mays (wrist) ahead of the bye week on Oct. 7.

 Although the defense was struggling, and Branch was pressing the issue, Campbell and the medical staff refused to rush him back into action until they felt he was fully ready.

 "I told Dan like, 'I'm starving' since I got injured," Branch said. "Just been day by day. Just been working, just been grinding. Showing up at 7 a.m."

 Branch, 24, was placed on the reserve/PUP list, meaning he would miss at least the first four games of the season after suffering a season-ending Achilles injury in 2025 that sidelined him throughout training camp and the preseason.

 He suffered the torn Achilles in Week 14 during the fourth quarter of the Lions' 44-30 win over the Dallas Cowboys and had to be carted off the field. He underwent surgery last December and his recovery period was projected to take eight to 12 months.

 Even with him being back, the Lions will try to remain conservative with his workload on Sunday after being away for so long.

 "Yeah, I think that'd be asking a lot to say he's going to play 70 plays, but we do feel like he can handle quite a bit here and we're going to push him in practice here early," Campbell said.

 Detroit will benefit from Branch's presence after the defense gave up at least 30 points in three of its first four games.

 

 Although the unit enjoyed a much better performance against Arizona on Oct. 11, the biggest struggles have been in the secondary where they've given up a league-high 1,487 passing yards. Branch feels he's "ready to go" after shaking off the rust during practice and remains confident he can help.

 "I just know what these group of guys are made up of and we all want the same thing. We all got the same goal," Branch said. "And we know that we've been shooting ourselves in the foot and shoot, we go hard each and every day. ... if you've got hard work, you're going to overcome a lot of things."

 Branch, a 2024 Pro Bowler, was drafted by the Lions in the second round of the 2023 NFL draft out of Alabama. He is eligible for a contract extension while playing on the final season of his rookie deal.

 In 2025, Branch started in all 12 of his appearances, logging 75 tackles, nine passes defended and five quarterback hits as one of the team's top defenders. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is also itching to work Branch back into the rotation.

 

 "Listen, I don't even know the word for it. I don't. But I mean, how many positions can he play and how fast?" Sheppard said. "I mean, he's a dynamic player. That is an elite player in this league, which we all know, guys. I'm not telling you nothing you don't know. That is an elite player in this league. But we also got to do right by the player."

 Mays suffered his wrist injury during training camp and was placed on injured reserve. He was projected to miss eight to 10 weeks and is on track to reenter the mix. Mays was acquired during the offseason to help the offensive line after spending his first four seasons with the Carolina Panthers . Campbell this week confirmed that Mays will likely start at center against the Packers although veteran OL  Juice Scruggs  has played well in his absence. Mays went through practice with quality reps and Campbell feels comfortable with bringing him back in that starting role, while Scruggs will swing between center and guard.

 "We would like to just rip this Band-Aid off of Cade," Campbell told 97.1 The Ticket on Wednesday morning. "I thought he had some good work yesterday. I thought he looked pretty good."

 With the Lions at 3-2, Campbell feels the returns have the team in good shape as it enters its first divisional matchup this season.

 Detroit went 2-4 against NFC North opponents last season after going 15-3 from 2022-24, which was tied with the Chiefs for the best intra-division record in the NFL, per ESPN Research.

 "I mean, we already kind of have a range of what we're looking at for him and for Cade a little bit," Campbell said. "We're still back and forth on what do we do with him? Do we work he and Juice in and out? In the center position, that's where it's a little different than a guard. That's somebody that's constantly touching the football."

title: The case for (and against) the Colts keeping Shane Steichen
summary: With GM Chris Ballard gone, can Steichen avoid following him out the door?
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS -- Losses were mounting, and the future was increasingly uncertain.

 As the Indianapolis Colts sputtered on their way to a seven-game losing streak to conclude their 2025 season, speculation turned to whether the team's head coach and others might be fired.

 Meanwhile, in other cities, a different conversation was happening. Colts coach Shane Steichen was also a topic of discussion for other teams. Some had interest in speaking with him about their own potential job openings.

 

 One team that filled an opening in the last hiring cycle had even identified Steichen as one of its top targets had he been fired, an executive from that club told ESPN.

 Now, speculation about Steichen's job is again at the forefront following Monday's decision by the Colts to dismiss general manager Chris Ballard. Given the words of primary owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon after last season -- she put Ballard and Steichen on notice and suggested this was a make-or-break year for both -- it's natural to assume Steichen might be next to go.

 But for now, he's still here. And there are many around the league who think he's a good coach in a bad situation. Some even believe one of the reasons Colts ownership hesitated to clean house after last season was a reluctance to part with Steichen.

 With the firing of Ballard, the Colts have -- for the time being -- decoupled the pair. Whether Steichen gets a reprieve remains to be seen. But at minimum, he has a chance to redeem himself.

 "I'm grateful for every day that I'm in this building, and I don't take that for granted," he said Monday. "I've got to get these guys ready for the Vikings."

 Per usual, Irsay-Gordon will be closely assessing what's happening at Colts headquarters. She'll be at practices this week and in meetings as the Colts prepare for Sunday's game at Minnesota. And she'll be listening to traffic on the coaches' headsets during the game, as she does each week in her efforts to gain insight.

 In her statement released Monday, she insisted that her family's evaluation will continue during the remainder of the season.

 "I also want to be clear," she wrote. "This decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve and win football games."

 So is there a scenario in which Steichen can survive? Should he?

 The case for Steichen 

 Steichen's debut season in 2023 is, perhaps, the best example of his coaching prowess. He took over a team that had gone 4-12-1 the year before he was hired, started the year with rookie quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr ., finished it with Gardner Minshew under center and still came within one play of winning the AFC South in the final week of the season.

 Steichen guided that team to six wins in its final nine games, losing to Houston in a season finale that decided the division.

 His overall record of 27-30 is not stellar. But it can be argued that Steichen has consistently gotten a lot out of a little with the Colts.

 He has started eight different quarterbacks in his three-plus seasons in Indianapolis. Among them are Joe Flacco and Philip Rivers, who remarkably came out of retirement to fill in after Daniel Jones sustained a ruptured Achilles last season.

 

 Still, Indianapolis ranks eighth in points per game since Steichen arrived (24.3), putting them ahead of teams with quarterback stability like the Philadelphia Eagles and Green Bay Packers . Since 2023 under Steichen, who is the team's offensive playcaller, the Colts rank in the top half of the league in offensive expected points added, yards per play and yards per game.

 The Colts have done this despite their quarterbacks under Steichen posting a collective QBR of 52.5, which ranks 19th in the NFL in that span.

 What might Steichen be capable of with a retooled roster and a quarterback he can build around?

 The case against Steichen 
 The quarterback issues Steichen has had to overcome are in some ways missteps of his own making. 

 The Richardson situation is a prime example. Steichen benched Richardson midway through the 2024 season, only to reinsert him into the starting lineup three weeks later after Flacco struggled. Steichen's position was that Richardson needed to prepare for games more intensely, but the coach articulated it poorly, leaving a disconnect between Richardson and the team.

 

 This came after Steichen was among the biggest advocates in the organization for drafting Richardson in 2023, even though he is among the least-experienced college quarterbacks ever drafted in the first round.

 Now, Steichen's quarterback decisions are again a subject of debate. The Colts, lacking great options at quarterback coming out of 2025, committed publicly in January to re-signing Jones despite his December Achilles injury. The Colts went all-in, signing Jones to a two-year, $88 million contract.

 It remains a middle-of-the-pack quarterback contract in terms of yearly average, but it was a commitment nonetheless. And Steichen's fingerprints were all over it, with the Colts buying into his belief that he could get Jones back to the career-best level he played at last season.

 Instead, Jones is struggling. He ranks 30th in QBR and 29th in yards per attempt and completion rate. Steichen backed him again Monday, saying he will continue to be the team's starter. But if there isn't improvement, Steichen could be faced with a decision as Richardson is still available on the bench.

 Then there is Steichen's overall performance. His teams have fared terribly against opponents with winning records. Just seven of his 27 wins with the Colts came against teams with winning records. Steichen also has a 9-11 record in division games.

 Ballard's fate has already been decided. The rest of this season might determine whether Steichen can achieve a different outcome.

title: Xavier Worthy proving to be an important piece for Chiefs
summary: Nate Taylor breaks down how important Xavier Worthy will be for the Chiefs vs. the Seahawks.

title: Kansas City Chiefs WR Xavier Worthy thriving in expanded role as Seahawks loom
summary: The Chiefs will likely need similar improved play -- or even better -- from Worthy in Sunday's showdown vs. Seattle.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- When  Chiefs  receiver Xavier Worthy entered Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday, he knew the team's offensive game plan was different for him.

 "They told me all week it's going to be for me, and I've got to step up for the receiver room," Worthy said of the coaching staff following the Chiefs' Week 6 win against the Los Angeles Chargers . "Guys are down, so I did my job."

 The proof was demonstrated in the Chiefs' opening possession. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes ' first passing attempt was for Worthy. As the game progressed, the Chiefs' need for Worthy to have a strong performance increased. Tight end Travis Kelce , Mahomes' most reliable pass catcher, sustained a right ankle injury in the first quarter.

 

 Mahomes responded by trusting Worthy -- and the receiver kept rewarding the Chiefs. In his best performance of the season, Worthy, a third-year player, finished Sunday's game with a game-high seven receptions for 73 yards. The Chiefs' offense needed Worthy's production, too, especially since it was Mahomes' first game this season without his top receivers: Tyquan Thornton , who was placed on injured reserve last week after suffering a dislocated left ankle, and Rashee Rice , who is recovering from a strained right hamstring.

 Worthy on Wednesday compared getting targets early in Sunday's game that led to positive receptions when a basketball player swishes multiple shots in the first quarter.

 "You hit five in a row [in basketball], it doesn't get any better than that," Worthy said, smiling. "It obviously built the confidence and led to a strong game."

 The 5-0 Chiefs will likely need similar play -- or even a better performance -- from Worthy in this Sunday's showdown against the Seattle Seahawks  (3-3), the NFL's defending champion.

 

 For much of his career, Worthy has tried to become the speed threat many had hoped after he broke the record for the 40-yard dash at the 2024 NFL combine (4.21 seconds). He showed sizable improvement as a rookie, recording 638 receiving yards and nine total touchdowns. But last season was a disappointment. He sustained a significant right shoulder injury on opening night when he collided with Kelce while running a crossing route.

 Coach Andy Reid acknowledged the Chiefs had to adjust the routes Worthy ran last season to better protect his shoulder. He finished with 532 receiving yards and one touchdown.

 "People look at him because he's a little bit smaller and he's real fast, so they think of him as just a deep threat," Reid said of Worthy, who is listed at 5-foot-11 and 165 pounds. "We've always looked at him like he can run shallow crosses, deep crosses. He can do all that stuff and [is] very good at it. He's tough and he's smart, so you can move him around a lot in a lot of different spots."

 In Sunday's game, Worthy caught the ball on crossing routes, beating zone and man-to-man coverage on different snaps. When the Chiefs asked him to work in the intermediate area of the field, he was able to create proper separation. All told, he led the team with 28 routes.

 Worthy never dropped the ball, either. He made multiple diving catches, becoming the Chiefs' first pass catcher this season to have a plus-17.1% catch rate over expected and a 100% catch rate with at least five targets, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 "Xavier had another good day," Mahomes said Sunday. "If he keeps stacking those, it'll help out a ton, as we get Rashee back."

 In September, Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy called plays that manufactured short receptions for Worthy, hoping his speed could be used to create explosive gains. Instead, Worthy was unable to outrun defenders or break tackles on the perimeter. In the Chiefs' first three games, he recorded 10 receptions on 15 targets for just 63 yards.

 The biggest moment for Worthy during that month was when he ran a deep route on opening night against the Denver Broncos . Instead of running his route in front of the two safeties, he kept sprinting to split the defenders in hopes Mahomes would throw a deep pass for him to run under. Instead, Mahomes threw an intermediate pass that was intercepted.

 "I thought one thing, he thought the other," Worthy said the following week of his miscommunication with Mahomes. "We both weren't wrong, but it's about getting on the same page and knowing what each other is going to do. It was a newer play that we didn't get a lot of reps of, so it's about understanding what [Mahomes] would rather like in [that] situation."

 

 Since the calendar flipped to October, Worthy has been a more effective receiver. The Chiefs beat the Las Vegas Raiders in part because Mahomes was able to find receivers downfield against man-to-man coverage. Worthy ran a deep over route when the Raiders blitzed in the first quarter and made a contested catch for a 41-yard gain.

 "I'm building momentum," Worthy said. "As a receiver, just getting that momentum and getting that first catch. That first deep ball, I felt like that's what unlocked it for me -- and I feel they trust me, just going out there and executing. Having the trust of your team is big."

 Worthy's role should continue to grow since Thornton is expected to be out until January.

 "Me and Pat [are] building that relationship and [it's] me feeling stronger and better each and every week, just continuing to be that reliable target for Pat and making his job easier," Worthy said Wednesday. "If I go out there and do that, everything's going to come."

 With more opportunities from Mahomes likely, Worthy is eyeing the first 100-yard receiving game of his career. After beating the Chargers, Worthy was satisfied to make a bigger impact in the Chiefs' continued success.

 "We're 5-0 -- and it's hard to be 5-0 in this league," Worthy said. "I feel like we're playing some of our best ball. Whatever I can do, whether it's getting targets or not, or taking two [defenders] or blocking in the run game for [running back  Kenneth Walker III ], I'm going to do it."

title: Fantasy football buzz: What to expect from J.J. McCarthy in first Giants start
summary: Just a few weeks after trading for the 2024 first-rounder, the Giants will start him against the Texans.
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 
 Oct. 21: J.J. McCarthy named Giants' starting QB for Week 7 
 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 The inevitable has finally arrived in New York: McCarthy is reportedly going to start at quarterback for the Giants in Week 7 .

 It was a decision destined to happen at some point following McCarthy's Sept. 28 acquisition from the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick. And it was a decision almost assuredly destined to happen this week after the Michigan product delivered 16.52 fantasy points in the fourth quarter alone, nearly leading his Giants to a comeback from down 34-10 to the Saints.

 McCarthy's installation doesn't promise any miracles, not for the Giants and not for fantasy, but it's an understandable, aggressive move that could positively shift the team's offensive dynamic.

 

 First off, don't take McCarthy's Week 6 performance remotely to heart, as it's almost entirely meaningless for evaluative purposes. High-scoring relief efforts by quarterbacks aren't uncommon. Since 2021, there have been 13 relief performances of 15 or more fantasy points by quarterbacks who made a start later in that season; that group averaged 5.2 fewer fantasy points as starters than in that relief appearance.

 More relevant to McCarthy's cause is his extensive tape from his 10 mediocre (to say it gently) starts in Minnesota last season. In those starts, he was 28th in Total QBR (36.1), 30th in completion rate (57.6%), 28th in off-target rate (19.3%) and 30th in touchdown-to-interception ratio (0.9). He struggled mightily when throwing into crowded spaces, with the fourth-worst passer rating when targeting a receiver with three or fewer yards of separation, per Next Gen Stats.

 What McCarthy did do that could have fantasy relevance, however, was aim deep about as often as any quarterback in the league. His average depth of target of 8.8 yards led all quarterbacks who started at least half of their teams' games, though he did have seven interceptions on throws of at least 15 yards, putting his skill set into the extreme risk/reward category. Anyone who watched Sunday's game can attest to that, as McCarthy was chucking the ball in a desperate attempt to breathe some life into a Giants offense that, to that point, had shown barely any.

 Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely each scored more than half of their Week 6 fantasy points after McCarthy entered the game, and the two combined for five catches on six targets for 130 yards and a touchdown on throws of at least 10 yards from McCarthy. Simply put, the upside is higher for both receivers with McCarthy under center, and that's especially relevant in a week with four teams on bye and the Giants facing an actually strong matchup against the Houston Texans defense. It's the fifth-most favorable matchup for wide receivers, when adjusted for the schedule.

 Beyond those occasional highlight moments, also expect some ugly days for McCarthy, Nabers, Likely and anyone from the Giants' offense, depending on the quarterback's play, the matchups themselves and the current state of the running game. Cam Skattebo 's last-minute role reduction (six snaps, no touches) thrust the offense into chaos last week, so we'll see how that plays out this week.

 I've got McCarthy as my No. 21 quarterback in Week 7, which is a borderline superflex/2QB starter, though his upside could make him a stronger situational option than, say, Kirk Cousins against the Los Angeles Rams , if your lineup demands that.

 

 NFL Nation:  Adonai Mitchell  returns to Jets practice 

 By Rich Cimini 

 The Jets' WR, sidelined the last four games with an injured finger on his right hand, returned to practice Wednesday on a limited basis -- his first practice since Sept. 25. His availability for Sunday against the Dolphins is a "pain tolerance issue," according to head coach Aaron Glenn. During the brief media period at practice, Mitchell seemed reluctant to use his right hand on one pass play in particular. If he's active for the game, he'd probably join  Garrett Wilson and Omar Cooper Jr . in three-receiver sets.

 

 

 Oct. 21: Are TEs more productive on National Tight Ends Day? 
 

 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 A note to Brock Bowers , Sam LaPorta , Juwan Johnson and all fellow tight ends: On Sunday, stand up and celebrate! It's National Tight Ends Day!

 To their fantasy managers: You can all sit down. There's not much to see here.

 Formally adopted as an NFL "holiday" beginning in 2019, National Tight Ends Day occurs on the fourth Sunday of October, as a way of honoring the position. This year, there is a 12-game slate on that day. Surely there'll be additional attention to the position on the highlight reel. For example, last season, Tucker Kraft and George Kittle celebrated their day with touchdowns , bringing it additional attention.

 But from a fantasy perspective, historically speaking, National Tight Ends Day doesn't specifically inflate tight ends' production, at least not to decidedly actionable levels.

 In the past seven seasons it has been celebrated (2019-25), tight end production was up only 0.29 fantasy points per game on October's fourth Sunday relative to the rest of the season, a differential as easily explained by random variance as by any additional boost provided by the now-annual event. Additionally, tight end usage was nearly identical to the numbers across the rest of the season, from routes run to target rate to red zone target rate to touchdowns scored.

 There's only one area where a benefit seems apparent recently. Across the past three seasons, tight ends rostered in more than half of ESPN leagues at the time of National Tight Ends Day saw a boost of 3.65 fantasy points per game relative to the rest of their seasons. This was almost entirely due to the group seeing a noticeable, 17% boost in red zone target production, resulting in their touchdown rates more than doubling (0.66 per game, compared to 0.31 the rest of the season).

 The small sample caveat naturally applies, since this was a group of 38 tight ends across three seasons. Additionally, across that same group, only three of their 40 best single-game totals from 2023-25 came on National Tight Ends Day. Is it possible that prominent tight ends are experiencing increasingly greater usage and attention on National Tight Ends Day as the holiday gains exposure across the league? Perhaps, and it's certainly something we're monitoring.

 Is it something we should account for in our fantasy lineup planning? Well, no, not necessarily.

 That said, if you're more moved by the data points, or if you're facing a razor-thin call at your flex spot between a tight end and a slightly more favorably projected running back or wide receiver, leaning tight end isn't an outrageous idea. Starting Mark Andrews (projected for 8.8 fantasy points in a favorable matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals ) over Rome Odunze (projected for 10.2 in a less-ideal matchup against the New England Patriots ) is a defensible move. Perhaps Lamar Jackson -- or Tyler Huntley , if Jackson is again out for Week 7 -- might choose to "celebrate" the occasion by giving Andrews that one additional red zone look he needs to hit paydirt.

 Aside from that, sit back, enjoy the day, and here's hoping we see a third straight 20-point Isaiah Likely game and continued fantasy TE1 production from Kyle Pitts Sr ., regardless of what the calendar tells us!

title: Six games in, are the Rams undisciplined or unlucky?
summary: The Rams' past three games (one win, two loses) have come down to the final play.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- After the Rams' Week 6 loss to the Arizona Cardinals dropped Los Angeles to 2-4 on the season, safety Quentin Lake had a reminder for a few of his teammates.

 We've been here before. 

 Three seasons ago, the Rams were 3-6 during their Week 10 bye. Los Angeles won seven of their last eight games to finish 10-7 and the No. 6 seed in the playoffs.

 The next season, the Rams were 1-4 during their Week 6 bye. They lost only three games the rest of the way to finish 10-7, win the NFC West and make a run as the No. 4 seed.

 "We found a way," Lake said. "So it's still early in the season. We got a lot of ball left to play, and I think guys are still motivated, everybody's still connected."

 The Rams have a favorable stretch coming up before their Week 11 bye, with their next four games coming against teams with a combined six wins: The 3-3 Las Vegas Raiders in Week 7 ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ), followed by the 0-6 Los Angeles Chargers , 1-4-1 Washington Commanders and 2-4 Cardinals.

 The Rams' past three games (one win, two losses) have come down to the final play. Though the games were close, veteran tight end Tyler Higbee said, they've also been full of moments when the Rams are "hurting ourselves, sometimes in critical moments, especially offensively."

 

 Lake said the focus now has to turn to "having the competitive stamina to make sure that we're being disciplined enough to get those wins."

 "Our past three games have all been decided on the last play, which has been wild," Lake said. "... And at the end of the day, it's how can we put ourselves in better positions to make sure that we don't have to even be in those positions? We don't have to make it where it comes down to the last play or a fourth-quarter drive or anything like that."

 After the loss to the Cardinals, Rams coach Sean McVay said he's "not really sure" why the self-inflicted wounds, like penalties, continue to be a problem.

 "I've continued to talk about it," McVay said. "We try to be able to harp on it. We've got to be able to figure it out and I don't have those answers right now. ... We've had some really critical errors at really unfortunate times. That's what our narrative has been for this year. We can't keep saying, 'Oh, that we haven't done that before.' Well, this year we are doing it. We have to be able to fix it."

 On Monday, McVay was asked whether he thought the Rams looked like an undisciplined team at times.

 "I can't deny that because we had some critical moments in critical situations," McVay said.

 If the Rams are going to "be able to not beat ourselves," as McVay said, they're going to have to do it while missing some key starters because of injury. In the Rams' loss to the Cardinals, Los Angeles lost nose tackle Poona Ford for the season after he ruptured his triceps, defensive end Kobie Turner for "a handful of weeks" because of a groin strain, wide receiver Davante Adams for six to 10 weeks because of a hamstring injury and kicker Blake Grupe for the season because of a torn ACL.

 The injuries have been a blow to a group still without defensive end Myles Garrett , who has sat out the Rams' past five games after needing mid-September knee surgery. Garrett is eligible to come back from injured reserve after sitting out the minimum four games, but McVay said Monday the Rams would not open his practice window this week.

 Lake said he doesn't think there's "a sense of panic" in the building after the slow start, but that "there has to be a sense of urgency in terms of making sure that we're putting ourselves in position to do the right things."

 The Rams entered the season as 5-1 favorites at DraftKings to win the Super Bowl. After McVay announced the injuries, their odds fell to 12-1.

 Entering Week 7, ESPN Analytics gives the Rams a 36% chance to make the playoffs, and less than a 1% chance to win an NFC West led by the undefeated San Francisco 49ers . McVay said he didn't think the Rams played the way they were "capable of" in Week 6, but despite the injuries, the team is "going to continue to fight."

 "We're going to continue to swing," McVay said. "These moments force you to learn a lot about yourself and about the people around you. ... We're looking to see us play better quality football, continue to establish identities that we feel like are in alignment with suiting our players the best that we can.

 "It's unfortunate that a couple of those guys are out, but we're going to continue to work. We have to be able to fight and that's exactly what we're going to do."

title: Why are the Raiders struggling in the second half of games?
summary: What's behind the Raiders' second-half struggles and what's next?
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Following the Las Vegas Raiders ' 33-30 home loss to the Buffalo Bills in Week 6, coach Klint Kubiak uttered a three-letter phrase in a vexed tone.

 The Raiders had lost their third straight game. And unlike their 45-17 loss in Week 5 to the New England Patriots , when the game felt decided by halftime, the Raiders went toe-to-toe with Buffalo, a Super Bowl contender, but their struggles in the second half, particularly in the third quarter when they were held scoreless, proved the difference-maker.

 When Kubiak was asked how the team can improve and get out of their current rut, he said the Raiders need to "close games out."

 

 That has been an issue for the Raiders in recent weeks. Yes, the Raiders are scoring more points than last season, and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins has played at a surprisingly high level, but their inability to finish games strong has hurt the Silver & Black. In the past three weeks, the Raiders have been outscored 64-41 in the second half and 24-3 in the third quarter.

 Multiple factors have contributed to their struggles in the second half, from inconsistent red zone production on offense to the defense allowing explosive plays in crucial moments. Kubiak said the team needs to clean up their act in the second half, starting on Sunday afternoon against the Los Angeles Rams ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ), if they want to have success that mirrors the first three weeks of the season when they went 3-0.

 "Overall, it's just a complete lack of production. It's really putting us in a bad spot as a team, not getting it done [and] getting outscored in the third quarter," Kubiak said Monday.

 The Raiders' third-quarter issues were a common theme in postgame talks against Buffalo. Cousins and wide receiver Tre Tucker said the frequent three-and-outs to begin the second half have been a momentum killer.

 

 That was certainly the case last week. With the game tied at 13 at the start of the third quarter, the Raiders failed to push the ball down the field. Cousins threw three straight incompletions, and the Raiders were forced to punt.

 The Bills did the opposite. They scored 10 unanswered points to take a double-digit lead. Buffalo had a nine-play, 47-yard drive that ended in a field goal. After Cousins threw an interception, Bills quarterback Josh Allen marched his team into the red zone where his wizardry was on display. Allen evaded multiple defenders and then threw a 12-yard shovel pass to wide receiver Keon Coleman to take a 23-13 lead with 6:22 to go in the third.

 The Raiders have committed seven turnovers in the second half this season. Four of Cousins' five interceptions have occurred in the final two quarters.

 "We can't come out flat," Tucker said. "Especially when we win the coin toss and defer, and we want the ball in the second half. We have not been great at doing that. ... That's a part of our winning formula."

 The opening sequence was almost similar to the one Las Vegas had against the Patriots. Down by 21 points, the Raiders needed a spark to keep some hope alive. Instead, they watched running back Ashton Jeanty record two short-yardage attempts, Cousins threw an incompletion, and A.J. Cole had to punt the ball away.

 Cousins said the Raiders are a "much better team" if they can start the third quarter more efficiently.

 

 "We have not played good football for the most part [in the third quarter]," Cousins said. "I mean, maybe one game had a better start to the third quarter, but we've got to be much, much better coming out."

 The margin for error is thin. And the Raiders need to do a better job of capitalizing on red zone opportunities. Overall this season, the Raiders have been fairly solid in the red zone. They have converted 63.6% of their red zone opportunities -- tied for 13th in the league.

 However, Las Vegas left points off the board by going 2-for-5 in the red zone against the Bills. The Raiders had a chance to score a touchdown early in the fourth quarter, but right guard Caleb Rogers whiffed on a block, and Jeanty was stopped for a 3-yard loss near the goal line. Two plays later, the Raiders had to kick a field goal to cut the deficit to 23-16.

 Against the Kansas City Chiefs  in Week 4 , the Raiders had a chance to extend their lead to six or 10 points during the early stages of the third quarter. Kicker Matt Gay nailed a 41-yard field goal, but the Chiefs were penalized for illegal formation, turning a fourth-and-7 into a fourth-and-2. Kubiak went aggressive and sent the offense back on the field, but Cousins' pass attempt to Jeanty was broken up by linebacker Drue Tranquill , leading to a turnover on downs.

 "We got to come away with those plays and get the touchdown, not the kick [a] field goal," Cousins said. "Those are all the plays throughout the game that you look back on, and you say, it didn't give us a chance to win. You got to make plays and be smart and manage the game well. And if you do that, you'd like to think that you give yourself a chance to close it out in the fourth quarter."

 The regression of the defense has factored into the Raiders' issues in finishing games strong. Las Vegas is near the bottom in almost every major statistical defensive category. The Raiders are 26th in points allowed per game (27), 28th in total yards allowed (371.7) and 25th in EPA by a defense (minus-18.55).

 Specifically in the second half, the Raiders' defense hasn't been great. Las Vegas has given up 15.3 points (27th) and 184.5 total yards (28th) in the second half.

 

 "Overall, if you're going to win the game, it's about limiting points, and we have to limit points in the red zone," Kubiak said.

 The Raiders understand they are close. Las Vegas was close to defeating the Chiefs and Bills in its past two home games. And despite having one of the worst rushing attacks and wide receiver rooms in the league, the Raiders are still sixth in points per game (26.7). That suggests they are heading in the right direction, and perhaps a bit closer to reaching their potential, especially on offense, than expected.

 Still, close is not enough.

 "At the end of the day, we don't want a moral victory. There's no stat for that. There's no column for it," Rogers said. "... We've got to close."

title: Miami Dolphins, New York Jets have clear plans for future success
summary: New York and Miami are rebuilding in 2026, but ahead of their matchup there's light at the end of the chaos.
full_text:
In the AFC East, you've got your MVP caliber quarterbacks, your big name coaches, your division winners.

 Then, there's the other guys.

 The New England Patriots and Buffalo Bills have won every division title since 2008. In fact, they've won all but three AFC East titles since the turn of the century. Meanwhile, the New York Jets and Miami Dolphins have combined for 19 winning seasons in the past 25 years, and haven't both finished above .500 since 2008.

 

 The Jets (2-4) and Dolphins (0-5) are rebuilding in 2026, but ahead of their matchup this Sunday (1 p.m., E.T., CBS) there's a light at the end of the chaos for each franchise.

 New York is in its second year under coach Aaron Glenn, after an ugly 3-14 season in which it failed to record a single interception (an NFL first), and general manager Darren Mougey. Sensing the direction the season was going, the Jets traded two of their premier players -- cornerback Sauce Gardner and defensive tackle Quinnen Williams -- landing three first-round picks in return.

 If they use them all, the Jets could end up taking six total players in the first round over two years, accelerating a rebuild while still keeping their core players under team control.

 New York moved on from Justin Fields and Aaron Rodgers , their last two opening-day starters at quarterback before Geno Smith took over this season, and they are eating up $48 million of the cap space (about 16%) in dead money. More than 1,200 miles south, the Dolphins underwent their second rebuild of the past 10 years, jettisoning core veterans and hiring both a new general manager and head coach in the same offseason for the first time since 2016.

 Their moves earned them an NFL-record $180 million in dead cap this season, but also netted them enough draft capital to select a league-high 13 rookies in April's draft.

 Here's how both teams are rebuilding their young core in order to go from the other guys, to division contenders.

 

 

 The Jets' three first-round picks in 2026 already have produced five sacks, three touchdowns and two 100-yard receiving days, with each of them taking turns in the spotlight.

 Tight end Kenyon Sadiq was the first -- a 105-yard receiving performance in Week 3.

 In Week 5, edge defender David Bailey stepped to the forefront with a dominating, three-sack game.

 Next came wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr . in Week 6 -- 103 receiving yards in his first full game.

 It's almost as if the Jets orchestrated the whole thing, arranging a different coming-out party each week. While the breakouts haven't always translated to wins, they illustrate what the Jets are about.

 The future.

 The 2022 to 2026 draft classes have produced 11 starters and top backups, giving the Jets a talent pipeline filled with players in the 25-and-under category. They comprise the core of the team, a group that will be supplemented by three first-round picks in the 2027 draft.

 It's remarkable how the roster has flipped. In 2024, it was a win-now team, with older players such as Rodgers, Davante Adams , Tyron Smith, Mike Williams and Haason Reddick . At the time, Jets owner Woody Johnson called it his best roster in 25 years of ownership. It turned out to be a spectacular (and expensive) failure -- a 5-12 finish that resulted in an organizational reset.

 The Jets are enduring significant short-term pain with the hope of long-term success -- a blueprint created by Glenn and Mougey. The Glenn-Mougey regime is 5-18, one of the worst stretches in franchise history, but you're starting to see flowering on previously barren branches.

 Mougey's first draft class, 2025, has yielded three starters -- right tackle Armand Membou , tight end Mason Taylor and cornerback Azareye'h Thomas . Opposing scouts say Membou has elite potential.

 In addition to the Bailey-Sadiq-Cooper troika, the '26 crop has produced defensive tackle  Darrell Jackson Jr ., a rising reserve destined for a starting role. They've already played a total of 675 snaps.

 

 "A flamethrower," Glenn said of Bailey, the No. 2 overall pick.

 Sadiq?

 "He runs 4.3 [in the 40-yard dash], and he's not from this planet," veteran receiver Tim Patrick said.

 Cooper?

 "He's a playmaker," Smith said. "He finds ways to make catches -- the tough catches -- he makes them look easy."

 Rookie cornerback D'Angelo Ponds is developing slowly -- a second-round pick who missed training camp with a calf injury -- but he still factors into the team's future.

 The '25 and '26 drafts have combined with young holdovers from the previous regime to give the Jets a foundation. Players such as running backs Breece Hall and Braelon Allen , guard Joe Tippmann and left tackle Olu Fashanu -- all from the '22 and '23 drafts -- are 25-and-under players signed through at least 2027.

 Using the trade market, Mougey added young starters in nose tackle T'Vondre Sweat , 25, and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell , 24, both 2024 second-round picks. Mitchell arrived in the Gardner trade with the Indianapolis Colts , which brought back first-round picks in '26 (Sadiq) and '27.

 The Jets might be building something special, but everybody knows it's a quarterback-driven league and they have a giant question mark at the position.

 Smith, 36, is playing at an ordinary level (his QBR is 54.5, about four points below the league average), and he will be a free agent after the season. In all likelihood, they will use one of those high draft picks on a quarterback, hoping their choice can galvanize what they believe is an emerging roster.

 Mougey's predecessor, Joe Douglas, did an admirable job of building the roster, but he botched his two big quarterback moves -- drafting Zach Wilson second overall in 2021 (after trading away Sam Darnold ) and dealing for Rodgers in 2023. Those mistakes undermined years of handiwork.

 It's incumbent to get the quarterback decision right. It's a familiar refrain. Previous regimes, dating back 50 years to the Joe Namath era, have tried and failed.

 For now, Mougey likes his roster -- a blend of young players and "the right mix of veterans to help kind of mold some of these young guys and change the culture," he said in training camp.

 The plan is materializing, but they could use some wins for validation.

 

 

 When the Dolphins signed quarterback Malik Willis this offseason, he expressed excitement about the prospect of throwing to wide receiver Jaylen Waddle , the team's No. 1 option and one of the best big-play threats in the league.

 Five days later, Waddle was traded to the Denver Broncos in exchange for first-, third- and fourth-round picks. First-year general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan was transparent about why he parted ways with the only established receiver on his team.

 "Waddle is 27 years old. We're in an era where the market for receivers is through the roof," he said in March. "And eventually, the chickens are going to come to roost with that. And so when we hit our stride, I'm not sure that all meshed the way that we needed to mesh -- we're in a position with our roster where we need to get younger and cheaper."

 Sullivan and first-year coach Jeff Hafley have been clear about the team's vision in 2026; the season would be less about wins and losses, and more about shedding salary and developing their young core.

 Miami's first three picks -- offensive lineman  Kadyn Proctor and cornerback  Chris Johnson in the first round and linebacker  Jacob Rodriguez in the second -- have played a combined 913 snaps this season. But the level of rookie participation goes beyond Miami's top three picks.

title: Vikings praise Aaron Jones Sr.'s heart with Jordan Mason out
summary: Jones said he was proud knowing the team was counting on him and he "can still be an every-down productive back."
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The Minnesota Vikings should return to full strength at running back Sunday, when veteran Jordan Mason is expected to return from a fractured finger against the Indianapolis Colts  ( 1 pm. ET, CBS ). So now is the perfect time to understand and recognize what Aaron Jones Sr . achieved during Mason's four-game absence. 

 Jones, who turns 32 in December, pushed through perhaps the most grueling month of his 10-year career to play a key role in the Vikings' 5-0 start. 

 With rookie Demond Claiborne not yet ready for regular work, and veteran newcomer DeeJay Dallas earmarked mostly for special teams, Jones took 90% of the Vikings' running back carries and played 81% of the team's overall offensive snaps.

 His 85 carries and 97 total touches were second most in the NFL over that period, and they were by far the most he has accumulated in a four-game stretch during a single season of his career, according to ESPN Research. And Jones did most of it with a sprained MCL in his left knee, an injury he said he has suffered on two other occasions in previous seasons but had never been able to play through. 

 During a conversation Wednesday with ESPN, Jones acknowledged his pride in answering the call under unique circumstances.

 "They can measure your height," he said. "They can measure your weight. They can't measure your heart. That's something my dad taught me."

 

 The Vikings entered the season planning to rotate Jones and Mason as part of a revitalized running game. Mason took 15 carries and played 48% of the snaps in the Vikings' Week 1 victory over the Green Bay Packers , while Jones took 12 and played 43% of the snaps. 

 But Mason reported soreness the next day and soon underwent surgery. Had the injury occurred later in the season, the Vikings might have felt more comfortable moving Claiborne or Dallas into the rotation. But for Weeks 2-5, Jones was the only back coach Kevin O'Connell wanted to use. 

 Jones, however, didn't make it very far before encountering his own adversity, suffering the MCL injury in Week 2 against the Chicago Bears . He missed one series while he was being fit for a brace, and said he surprised himself by feeling well enough to continue in the game. In each of his previous sprained MCLs, Jones said he missed the remainder of the game and then at least another two weeks. 

 On this occasion, with the Vikings out of trustworthy options, he returned to close out the game with a 15-yard run for a first down. Afterwards, he found his emotions swelling as he sought out O'Connell.

 "I gave him hug and I was like, 'This s--- means something,'" Jones said. "This has been my life. This is what I came up on. So this is how I play."

 

 Pro football is rife with military metaphors and associated hyperbole. In this case, Jones' effort and commitment genuinely moved people throughout the Vikings organization. His return in Chicago, and then his willingness to push through residual soreness to play the next three games, left the normally loquacious O'Connell in a rare spot.

 "It's hard to even put into words," O'Connell said. "Just the toughness, the way he's been able to turn over after a high volume of carries and get to a place by the next Sunday with a lot of work, a lot of time in the recovery room and just knowing his body like he does. He's just been an absolute pro. He's been a warrior, and I'm just so thankful that we have Aaron Jones on our team."

 Said offensive coordinator Wes Phillips: "The word 'warrior' has been thrown out many times, but it certainly highlights his toughness, his love for the game, and his commitment to this team and his teammates."

 Jones split carries with teammates during much of his career with the Green Bay Packers , averaging 174 carries per season from 2017 to 2025. Were he to continue at his current rate this season, Jones would nearly double that average. 

 It almost certainly won't happen, given Mason's expected return, but Jones said he has demonstrated that even at this stage of his career, he can still provide credible games as a featured back. His 370 rushing yards during Mason's four-game absence were more than every NFL running back other than the Atlanta Falcons ' Bijan Robinson (497) and the Buffalo Bills ' James Cook (475).

 "I feel like I showed that age is just a number," said Jones. "I take a lot of pride in knowing that they were counting on me, and then just showing that, 'Hey, I can still be an every-down productive back given the circumstances or given the opportunity.'"

 

 It all bubbled to the surface in Week 5. Upset about a red zone fumble in the fourth quarter, he bulldozed over Saints safety Julian Blackmon and scored an 8-yard touchdown in fourth quarter to give the Vikings a 20-13 lead. He abandoned plans to perform a choreographed New Orleans-style dance and just let loose with a raw expression of emotion.

 "I feel like it was a culmination of four weeks of work," he said, "along with answering and overcoming that fumble. It was a straight passion. I blacked out and started screaming, yelling, beating my chest.

 "It was funny because after the game a couple of my buddies called me. They're from New Orleans. I played with them in college and they're like, 'Hey, we thought you were going to do a dance.' And I'm like, 'Bro, I blacked out. I just blacked out.'"

title: Things you don't know about Patriots running back Rhamondre Stevenson
summary: Stevenson does all the little things for the Patriots, and he's on the cusp of 100 carries for the sixth straight season.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- This isn't a matchup Rhamondre Stevenson is supposed to win. Not even close.

 Aligned to quarterback Drake Maye 's left and 2 yards in front of him, the New England Patriots running back has both hands on his thighs as he peers into the "B" gap between left tackle Will Campbell and left guard Walter Rouse .

 New York Jets linebacker Demario Davis is in an attacking stance at the line of scrimmage, the 28-yard line. As the ball is snapped on third-and-6, Davis turns suddenly to plow into the side of Campbell. He is trying to create a clear path for edge rusher Will McDonald IV , who is looping behind him from his wide alignment, to get to Maye.

 Except ...

 The 6-foot, 227-pound Stevenson makes initial contact with Davis with a two-handed shove, slides to his right and then drives his hands into the chest of the 6-4, 245-pound McDonald. This stops McDonald's path towards Maye. And with plenty of time in the pocket, Maye completes a 39-yard pass downfield to receiver  DeMario "Pop" Douglas .

 This play from last Sunday's home win exemplifies what Stevenson means to the Patriots. He is one of the NFL's best running backs in pass protection , endearing himself to teammates as a quiet presence who is willing to do anything to help his team when he doesn't have the football in his grasp.

 

 "He's somebody I feel very strongly about and have since we drafted him [in 2021]. Great human being, high character. Very unselfish," offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said of the Patriots running back. "Need him to carry it 24 times? He'll carry it 24 times. Need him to block 16 blitzes? He'll block 16 blitzes. Need him to catch 10 passes? He'll catch 10 passes. Whatever we ask him is what he'll embrace with a great attitude and mindset. Very dependable. I think everybody in our offensive unit trusts him completely."

 While the Patriots rank sixth in rushing yards per game (130.7) this season, Stevenson is on the cusp of a franchise milestone entering Thursday's road game against the Chicago Bears ( Amazon Prime, 8:15 p.m. ET ). He needs 29 rushes to join Jim Nance (1965-1971), Sam Cunningham (1973-1979) and Tony Collins (1981-1987) as the only players in Patriots history with six straight seasons with 100 or more carries.

 Despite that sort of workload and this being Stevenson's sixth season in New England, he can still fly under the radar. With the Patriots (4-2) in the spotlight against the Bears (4-2), here are three things you might not know about the 28-year-old native of Las Vegas.

 Pass protector supreme 
 Stevenson has the third-most pass block wins (197) among running backs over the past five seasons, according to ESPN Analytics and NFL Next Gen Stats. Only the Rams' Kyren Williams (230) and Eagles' Saquon Barkley (227) have more. Maye calls him one of the Patriots' best players, saying he always does things the right way.

 Backup quarterback Tommy DeVito added: "It's comforting having somebody back there like him. I have had this feeling before with another running back and that was with Saquon [Barkley] -- you're not worried in pass protection. ... He's super smart, knows all the [defensive] looks and takes pride in it. As good as he is as a runner -- fourth all-time here now as a Patriot -- I think for quarterbacks it shows how much love he has for us."

 

 When head coach Mike Vrabel was hired in 2025, he said Stevenson's work stood out to him as a player he wanted to retain because it reflected the team identity he hoped to create.

 "I didn't know Rhamondre [but] the way he played without the football is usually a good indication of caring about the football team," Vrabel said this week.

 Stevenson highlights "90% wanting to do it and 10% knowing how to do it" as his formula for success in pass protection, crediting former coach Bill Belichick, McDaniels and former New England running back James White as primary NFL influences.

 "If you can protect on third down, you're going to play. That's what they would tell me," Stevenson said. "When we were doing walkthroughs, they would make sure my eyes were right. Even if a blitz wouldn't come, they would ask me who I have [to block if it did] to sharpen my skills. It's never really been how to do it, it's been about knowing who's coming, knowing the defense."

 The selfless play helps explain, in part, why he garners respect in the locker room.

 "It's like receivers going in to block. Receivers want to catch the ball and running backs want to run the ball," DeVito said. "So for him to take that kind of passion -- he stays late, watches extra film, make sure he's good on all the looks before practice and he's really in tune with -- I think that's the main thing that goes unnoticed about his game.

 "You see him in there and it's like, 'I know 'Mondre has got me.'"

 Ultimate teammate 
 Douglas, a fourth-year receiver, is one of Stevenson's closest friends on the team. Their bond initially formed, according to Douglas, because they saw a little of themselves in each other -- family-oriented and driven.

 But whereas Douglas has an exuberant personality reflected in his dancing touchdown celebrations, Stevenson is more reserved. His trademark celebration is to bring his hand toward his mouth before pointing to the sky after scoring.

 

 "He has that hard shell on the outside," Douglas said. "But he cares a lot, and I don't think a lot of people know that because he's a running back. He's quiet but very funny."

 Douglas shared a story from the team's Sept. 27 loss against the Jaguars, which was significant for him because it was his first NFL game in his native Jacksonville. He purchased 10 tickets.

 "I was like, 'Man, that's a lot of tickets. I'm not getting any more,'" said Douglas, a 2023 sixth-round pick in the final year of his rookie contract. "He was like, 'I got you, Pop.' It was 3-5 more tickets to help me out. That was real."

 Veteran tight end Hunter Henry 's connection to Stevenson is tied, in part, to them having the longest tenure with the Patriots among players on the active roster (along with defensive tackle Christian Barmore ). Henry is one of the few who can recall Stevenson announcing his presence as a rookie in the 2021 preseason opener with a 91-yard touchdown run late in the fourth quarter.

 "I was like, 'Oh wow, who is this guy? He has some juice.'" Henry recalled. "We've been together for a while, and the longer you're in this game, you realize how special the relationships in the locker room are, and that's a special one I've always enjoyed. He's quiet, but once you get to know him, he comes out of his shell a little bit."

 Stevenson shared that such "brotherhood" is what he appreciates about his Patriots tenure, and how he leans into that for motivational fuel.

 "I'm not the loudest person around but everything I want to attain, and the teammate I want to be and legacy I want to leave, I speak it out loud and tell my teammates. Then I want them to hold me accountable," he said.

 "Obviously, all of us can play football in here -- we're in the NFL -- but I want to be known as a great teammate that pays it forward. I love what Tommy said, that sigh of relief when I'm in the huddle, making someone's job easier. That's the goal."

 Fueled by his dad's memory 
 Stevenson credits his late father, Robert, for shaping his approach to football. He said it's a result of watching his father carry himself and the guidance he passed down.

 Robert, 54, died unexpectedly in March of 2025, and Stevenson has since honored his memory by wearing a bracelet with his ashes. When Stevenson posts on Instagram, it always includes the same message -- "RIP Pops" - with a black heart and the letters "AGTG" (all glory to God). Stevenson stayed in Las Vegas for an extended stretch of the 2025 offseason, mourning with his mother, Juran, along with his six siblings and extended family.

 

 Many teammates wanted to be there for him upon his return.

 "He's just a good…
