title: Senators fans booing Tkachuk reminiscent of previous unpleasant sports returns
summary: Brady Tkachuk isn't the first notable sports figure to be met with jeers by fans of his prior team.
full_text:
On Wednesday night, months of mixed emotions for Ottawa Senators fans came to a head as Brady Tkachuk made his first trip back to the Canadian Tire Centre as a member of the Florida Panthers .

 

 The Senators drafted Tkachuk in 2018, and he made three All-Star teams with the franchise. After being swept in the first round by the Carolina Hurricanes this past season, however, Tkachuk asked to be traded from the team so he could join his brother Matthew Tkachuk in Florida.

 Senators fans let him have it when he took the ice, showering him with boos.

 

 Tkachuk isn't alone in hearing the boo-birds on coming back to his former club, but if we were to include every contentious homecoming in sports, this article would drag on longer than an awkward encounter with your ex. Instead, we'll just regale you with some of the most memorable ones.

 

 Juan Soto in New York, 2025 

 Soto spent the 2024 season with the Yankees before landing a 15-year $765 million contract with the Mets in the 2024 offseason. What was Soto welcomed to as his first time to Yankee Stadium as a Met? A shower of boos.

 

 On top of that, every time Soto took the field on defense, Yankee fans also turned their backs on the right fielder.

 

 John Calipari in Lexington, 2025 

 Calipari spent a decade and a half leading the Kentucky Wildcats before trading blue for red and accepting the Arkansas Razorbacks job last spring. Kentucky went to the Final Four four times under Calipari -- capturing a national title in 2011-12 -- but finished in unceremonious fashion each of his past four seasons.

 The reaction when Calipari walked onto the court in his return to Lexington? A chorus of boos.

 

 

 James Harden in Philadelphia, 2023 

 

 Harden spent a season and a half with the Philadelphia 76ers before being traded to the LA Clippers in October 2023. He requested a trade during the 2023 offseason and later called 76ers president Daryl Morey a liar after not being traded initially.

 Philadelphia fans welcomed him as only they could -- booing Harden heavily during introductions and every time he touched the ball. They also cheered during his missed shots.

 

 LeBron James in Cleveland, 2010 
 

 James  went from being hailed as a hero to jeered as a villain quicker than the writers of "Game of Thrones." 

 The environment was nothing short of combative as James returned to Cleveland for the first time as a member of the  Miami Heat . The feelings of betrayal, disappointment and vitriol directed at him were tangible in the arena -- and in the city as a whole.

 LeBron hadn't just been the most popular sports figure in Cleveland, he was one of its own. So his departure for South Beach brought about a different level of anguish to the championship-starved city that had its hopes and dreams resting upon his shoulders.

 The "kid from Akron" was showered with boos and obscenities from former fans. Some of them threw things (including beverages and a battery); others held signs featuring things such as "Quitness" and "Witnessed No Championship," along with the more straightforward "I Hate LeBron." According to the team, four fans were ejected, and one was arrested that night.

 King James powered through the animosity to score 38 points en route to a 118-90 Heat win.

 LeBron would go on to regain Cleveland's love with a hard-earned Larry O'Brien Trophy in 2016.

 
 Jack Eichel in Buffalo, 2022 
 Eichel , a Vegas Golden Knights forward and former Buffalo Sabres captain, was traded in November 2022. He had zero points in Vegas' 3-1 loss at the KeyBank Center in March 2022 while being showered with boos from his former supporters.

 The return trip was a bit different , aside from the same raucous chorus of boos.

 Eichel had a hat trick in the Golden Knights' 7-4 win over the Sabres. That extended Vegas' win streak to nine games. This time, Eichel seemed to relish playing the heel.

 

 "I think last year I didn't know what to expect," Eichel said after the game. "I had an emotional connection -- I still do -- to this city and these people. I came in this year knowing what I was going to get and the kind of reception. I just tried to use the energy."

 
 Bryce Harper in Washington, 2019 
 

 From favored son to public enemy No. 1,  Harper , who left the  Washington Nationals  to sign a then- record-breaking 13-year, $330 million deal  with their National League East rival  Philadelphia Phillies  in February 2019, didn't garner an exceptionally warm welcome when he returned to Nationals Park for the first time.

 Fans showered him with boos during a pregame tribute video, then cheered loudly as ace  Max Scherzer  struck him out in his first at-bat. The heckling didn't sit well with Harper as he called fans out after the game, saying they " crossed the line ."

 Some will argue this reception was petty as Harper simply went to the highest bidder; others will say loyalty should count for something. 

 We'll just say this: The Nationals went on to win the World Series the season after he left.

 
 Kevin Durant in Oklahoma City, 2017 
 

 Golden State Warriors  vs.  Oklahoma City Thunder : A game to live in NBA infamy. No departure had caused such a ruckus around the Association since King James was hounded for "The Decision." 

 You didn't have to spend much time in OKC to see just how much  Kevin Durant  meant to the city -- the guy even had a restaurant named after him (the establishment closed in the wake of his departure but has since reopened with a different name and theme).

 Subsequently, the welcome KD received was far from friendly. There were deafening boos while he warmed up, when he was introduced and whenever he touched the ball on offense. There were also cupcake signs -- so many cupcake signs. Not to mention at least one fan dressed as an actual cupcake.

 To make matters worse, there was the messy divorce from his former teammate and friend,  Russell Westbrook , which added a whole other layer of animosity. Things got chippy between the ex-duo throughout the game, and they exchanged words on several occasions. At one point during the contest, Westbrook could be seen yelling: "I'm coming!" 

 Durant got the last laugh, though, dropping 34 points and grabbing nine rebounds as the Warriors secured a dominant 130-114 victory. After the game, he commented on the persistent boos, saying: "I actually thought it would be a little louder, but it was fun." 

 

 Deion Sanders in Atlanta, 1994 
 

 Sanders, who played for the  Atlanta Falcons  for five years, left the city outraged after signing with the  San Francisco 49ers . There was more ill will in the wake of his departure, as Falcons players claimed he demanded preferential treatment. They also said "Prime Time" really meant "Part Time" because Sanders split time between the  Atlanta Braves  and the Falcons.

 This heated homecoming tale was a bit dissimilar to the others: Rather than enduring the relentless ridicule during his return to the Georgia Dome, Sanders taunted the Falcons faithful.

 That's right, Prime Time flipped the script. He put on a show. It wasn't enough to high-step the final 40 yards into the end zone on a 93-yard interception return, he decided to turn sideways and flash a big ole grin toward the Atlanta bench for good measure. 

 The more they booed, the more he thrived (and danced).

 The 49ers would go on to win 42-3.

 

 Johnny Damon in Boston, 2006 
 

 All's fair in love and baseball -- except for leaving the  Boston Red Sox  for the  New York Yankees . You really just can't do it. We mean, you can, but you're going to get publicly reprimanded for it.

 One of the most heated rivalries in sports is not something to be trifled with, just ask Damon. The former Boston star was granted some leniency because of his involvement in bringing the Sox a World Series title, but the fans were still pretty brutal in his return to Fenway Park.

 Many of them opted to throw fake and real dollar bills on the…

title: Jameis Winston vs. J.J. McCarthy: Pros and cons of Giants' QBs
summary: Coach John Harbaugh must weigh the options in his QB conundrum, with two players who could start at Houston.
full_text:
Editor's note: This was originally published on Tuesday, a day before sources told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler that the Giants would start  J.J. McCarthy  on Sunday against the Texans. 

 EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants have a quarterback decision to make. 
 
 They can go with the veteran Jameis Winston , who just lost his first game as a starter this season, or the recently acquired and still somewhat unknown J.J. McCarthy on the road Sunday against the Houston Texans ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ). 
 
 Coach John Harbaugh declined to make a decision on Monday, although it does appear to be coming soon with the Giants (3-2-1) scheduled to have a team meeting Tuesday and their first practice of the week Wednesday. 
 
 Just when it appeared Winston had closed his vice grip on the starting job, McCarthy went out Sunday and opened some eyes with his fourth-quarter performance. He had 243 yards passing and led three scoring drives in less than 12 minutes. 
 
 "I thought he came in there and did a heck of a job given the circumstances," Harbaugh said. 
 
 Just like that, a quarterback conundrum was born, leaving Harbaugh with two realistic options to be his starting quarterback this week.   
 
 Here's a closer look at the decision: 
 
 
 

 

 

 Jameis Winston 

 
 
 Pros 
 
 
 Winston has been the quarterback ever since Jaxson Dart sustained his season-ending knee injury in the second quarter of the Giants' Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams . It has been an up-and-down five games for Winston, but Sunday against the Saints was his first loss in four starts. The Giants are 2-1-1 since Winston took over as the starter and are in first place in the NFC East. They aren't in a position where they need to make any panic moves, such as switching QBs. 
 
 Winston has seven touchdown passes and four interceptions in his four starts. So it's not as if the Giants have struggled to get into the end zone with him at quarterback. Only seven quarterbacks have thrown more touchdown passes than Winston during that span this season. 
 
 
 
 Winston also has done it without a consistent running game. The Giants are 22nd in the NFL, averaging just 3.8 yards per carry over the past four games. 
 
 What Winston does have in his back pocket is time on task with his top receivers: wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely . They've spent the past month getting on the same page. Nabers has three straight 100-yard games. Likely (383 receiving yards) is less than 100 yards shy of setting a new career high. It's only Week 7.  
 
 Nabers, Likely and the locker room have full confidence in Winston. They've already seen they can win games with him as the quarterback and watched him play at a relatively high level throughout his career. They know that's in him. 
 
 "We all believe in Jameis," fullback Patrick Ricard said. "Jameis puts everything into this. He's a great leader. We know what he's capable of but I guess we'll see."    
 
 
 
 
 Cons 
 
 
 The Jameis Winston experience. With Winston comes inconsistent plays and mistakes. His four interceptions are tied for fifth most since becoming the starter. His 45.6 QBR is 22nd among 30 qualifying quarterbacks. 
 
 So it's not as if Winston has played great. But he has played well enough to win games. It also should be noted that Winston's four starts were against the Titans, Cardinals, Commanders and Saints -- teams with a combined 6-17-1 record. The schedule is going to be much less forgiving from here on out, with matchups against the unbeaten 49ers, the division-leading Jaguars and Browns, and a strong Seahawks squad coming up.    
 
 If the Giants are dreaming about the potential for better quarterback play ... 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 J.J. McCarthy 
 
 
 
 Pros 
 
 
 The element of the unknown is perhaps McCarthy's most attractive trait. He has talent as a top-10 pick of the Minnesota Vikings in 2024, and who knows, there might be high-end quarterback play buried somewhere in there. 
 
 At the very least, McCarthy flashed that potential in his short stint Sunday. It was impressive. 
 
 So was McCarthy's ability to throw the ball deep downfield. He went 3-of-4 for 119 yards with a touchdown and no interceptions on passes of 20 air yards or more. Winston did not attempt any such passes against the Saints. 
 
 Harbaugh said he would judge the quarterbacks based on "performance." And it's hard to argue what McCarthy did leading the Giants on three scoring drives and close to a fourth even though it was in a helter-skelter football circumstance trying to rally in the final minutes. 
 
 McCarthy could also provide a much-needed boost to the running game. The Giants designed an offense for Dart filled with zone-reads and quarterback rollouts. That's better suited to McCarthy's game than Winston's. Harbaugh conceded that.  
 
 "The elements that we're talking about with some of the read plays and some of the different things you do moving the quarterback around," Harbaugh said, "those are definitely things that are part of the equation." 
 
 The Giants are looking for a way to jump-start their run game, and McCarthy might be it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Cons 
 
 
 A young and relatively inexperienced quarterback like McCarthy making his first start on the road against a defense like the Texans isn't ideal. Houston's defense hasn't been great this season, but it's still third in the NFL with 18 sacks and has perhaps the league's best pass rush duo with  Will Anderson Jr . and Danielle Hunter on the edges. 
 
 McCarthy has a 41.2% completion rate and minus-9.3 completion percentage over expectation (CPOE) under pressure since the start of last season. That ranks in the bottom half of the league among qualifiers. 
 
 Winston has a much more serviceable 50.0% completion rate and minus-0.4 CPOE. That would seem to give him a better chance against the Texans. 
 
 McCarthy also has had very few reps with Nabers and Likely, having arrived three weeks ago. 
 
 "You guys saw them," McCarthy said on Sunday, referring to the fourth quarter against the Saints. 
 
 They had almost no on-field working relationship prior to this past weekend. Only a few throws on the side at practice and pregame warmups.   
 
 It makes the bye week perhaps a better spot to make the switch (if necessary) to avoid the possibility of crushing McCarthy's confidence after an already rocky introduction to the NFL with the Vikings.

title: Bucs QB Jalon Daniels swaps jerseys with idol, Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers
summary: Following Pittsburgh's 26-19 overtime victory, Jalon Daniels left with a keepsake from his idol, Aaron Rodgers.
full_text:
TAMPA, Fla. -- All last week, teammates of Tampa Bay Buccaneers rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels urged him to do it.

 

 "I was talking to the quarterbacks beforehand and they basically were just like, 'If you get the opportunity to ask him, you better ask him,'" Daniels told ESPN.

 Fellow Buccaneers quarterback Brett Rypien told Daniels, "If you didn't ask him, I was going to ask for you," Daniels recalled.

 They were talking about Daniels meeting his idol -- Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers , who on Sunday led Pittsburgh to a 26-19 come-from-behind overtime victory  over the host Bucs -- and asking for a jersey.

 "Last season, last go around for him. So, I had to ask before he got up out of here," Daniels said, referring to Rodgers' plans to retire following the 2026 campaign.

 Daniels summoned the courage to do so and was met with a long embrace, which was captured on camera postgame and showed a tender side to Rodgers not often seen because of his intensity in games.

 

 "I mean, it was kind of crazy," Daniels said. "So, just kind of ... without trying to completely ask that -- I don't want to be that guy -- and he was just like, 'I know exactly what you're getting at. I'll give you the jersey.' And then I'm like, 'All right man, thank you.'" The pair shook hands. Daniels then heard something he never imagined: The Super Bowl winner and future Pro Football Hall of Famer wanted his jersey too.

 "[I] was about to walk away and he was like, 'Wait, hold on. Can I get yours?'" Daniels recalled Rodgers asking. "Now, that's kind of what caught me by surprise."

 What Daniels didn't know was how much Rodgers knew of and respected his game from afar. The week prior, the 2026 undrafted free agent led the Bucs to a 24-16 primetime upset at the Dallas Cowboys . It was the Bucs' first victory of the season and just Daniels' second career start, which came unexpectedly after starter Baker Mayfield suffered a dislocated right thumb in Week 3.

 "I appreciate the respect," Rodgers said of Daniels on the CBS broadcast. "Super respectful guy. I like his game. I like the way he throws it. Obviously, super talented with his feet. I'm excited to see how he develops. Learning behind a guy who's played a long time like Baker is obviously going to be great for him."

 Daniels was touched by the praise.

 "I respect that, as well," he said. "It's not every day you hear that from a Hall of Famer."

 

 Rodgers' ability to perform in high-pressure situations, make passes from different angles, get out of the pocket and throw off-platform were elements Daniels tried to bring to his own game as a six-year starter for  Kansas  -- after Daniels was initially supposed to redshirt. Daniels' career as a Buccaneer began in similar fashion by not hearing his name called at all during draft weekend and starting Bucs training camp fourth on the depth chart. He moved all the way up to No. 2 by beating out veteran Jake Browning  -- who had previously started 10 career games for the Cincinnati Bengals  -- by giving the Bucs an offensive spark in the preseason.

 Daniels said the moment with Rodgers "absolutely" lifted his spirits.

 At one point Sunday, Tampa Bay was leading 16-3. But Rodgers mounted a fourth-quarter comeback while the Steelers' defense clamped down. Daniels threw two fourth-quarter interceptions, and the Bucs fell to 1-5.

 "It wasn't easy," Daniels said, "but it comes with the game."

title: Raheem Morris is back in Atlanta -- and he's bringing his surging 49ers defense
summary: Raheem Morris is returning to Atlanta for the first time since being fired as head coach. And his tenure as the 49ers' defensive coordinator is off to an amazing start.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Upon his return to Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Sunday , Raheem Morris won't head toward the home locker room as the coach of the Atlanta Falcons . Instead, he will veer in the opposite direction as the San Francisco 49ers'  defensive coordinator.

 Six games into his tenure with the 49ers, Morris -- who spent the past two years as Atlanta's head coach -- isn't worried about how to get back into the top chair. His top priority is leading a surging defense that has already surpassed expectations. It's why, when asked last week whether he hoped to get a third crack at becoming a head coach, Morris quickly brushed the idea aside.

 "We have somewhere in society been screwed up," Morris said. "We have got this illusion in our head that everybody's a head coach. There are 32 head coaches in the National Football League. There are 32 defensive coordinators, and there are 32 offensive coordinators, and there's 32 everything we do. ... We are blessed and you couldn't have a better job than all of us."

 Morris' return to Atlanta provides an ideal backdrop to examine the effect he has had on a San Francisco defense that is on its fifth coordinator in as many years. With some minor but notable schematic changes to unlock a more aggressive secondary and productive front, his group provided game-winning sequences the past two weeks against Seattle and Washington . And the numbers through six undefeated weeks speak for themselves.

 

 This season, the 49ers have allowed the fewest explosive plays (rushes of 10-plus yards and passes of 20-plus yards) in the NFL. They rank fourth in points allowed per game (18.3) and yards allowed per play (4.7). They're also fifth in total yards allowed per game (300) and defensive expected points added (21.59), as well as seventh in ESPN's defensive efficiency metric (64.95).

 Most of that production has come without star DE  Nick Bosa ( calf ), as well as DT  Alfred Collins ( patellar tendon ), DT  C.J. West ( knee ) and DE  Sam Okuayinonu (foot). Which is why safety  Ji'Ayir Brown  said that with a little injury luck and more time on task with Morris, San Francisco's defense can be even better the rest of the way.

 "Honestly, I think we can be No. 1 in all categories, but it is a new defense," Brown said. "It is a lot of figuring things out."

 Brown's belief is rooted largely in the improvement of his position group. Despite the occasional hiccup, the Niners have continuity from last season at safety ( Malik Mustapha  and  Marques Sigle ) and cornerback ( Renardo Green , Deommodore Lenoir and Upton Stout ). During training camp, all players in the secondary pointed to Morris' schematic tweaks as allowing them to play more freely in coverage.

 Unlike previous coordinators with linebacker backgrounds, such as Robert Saleh and DeMeco Ryans, Morris comes with a long history working with defensive backs. Morris has spent nine NFL seasons working as either a defensive backs coach or a defensive pass game coordinator. He has also spent time coaching receivers, including with Atlanta in 2016 when Niners coach Kyle Shanahan was the team's offensive coordinator.

 "You can't help but bring that back to defense when you had to go back over there," Morris said about his time as an offensive coach. "When I was able to go back and really formulate how I see the game, how I feel the game, how you want to make your players feel the game, that philosophy really helped me a lot to grow."

 While Morris hasn't abandoned the Niners' long-held preference for zone coverage, he has tweaked it in subtle ways that have changed how his defensive backs attack. Under Saleh in 2025, the 49ers were in base defense -- three linebackers and four defensive backs -- on just 18.5% of snaps (29th-highest rate in the NFL). They played Cover 6 -- a combination of quarters coverage on one side of the field and Cover 2 on the other -- on 11.6% of snaps (ninth-highest rate).

 

 In part because of rookie linebacker  Jaden Dugger 's versatility, Morris now has the team in base defense on 37.7% of snaps (ninth-highest rate in the league). They're in Cover 6 on 19.2% of snaps (fifth-highest rate). Morris is also utilizing more "match" coverage, which asks defenders to start in traditional zone drops, keep their eyes on the quarterback and read routes to tighten up throwing lanes. If a pass catcher crosses into their path, the defender picks up that player, often only turning him loose for checkdowns and short gains.

 The approach has not only served to limit big plays, but it has also allowed the secondary to be more active. That was evident in Green's two-interception game in Seattle and Mustapha's jarring hits to help seal Monday night's win over Washington.

 "Those guys aren't counting on linebackers, so they have to be more aggressive in coverage," Shanahan said. "Those guys are playing concepts to stop plays without any help and that's been their edge. I think it's made them better. It's given them more confidence in practice, and I think that's what we're all seeing in games."

 With the pass rush, Morris has found ways to improve a unit that ranked last in sacks (20) and sacks per dropback (3.2%) in 2025. The defensive line has missed Bosa's presence for the majority of the season, but San Francisco has varied looks with five-down linemen, sometimes deploying Dugger as an extra edge rusher. The 49ers are still just 17th in sacks per dropback (6.4%) and tied for 12th in sacks (15), though their nine sacks over the past two weeks are second most in the NFL in that span. Last season, they didn't record their 15th sack until Week 13.

 The sack production is coming from all over in Morris' scheme; 11 players have contributed at least half of a sack. With defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa facing double-teams on 79% of his snaps (19th most in the NFL), Morris moves him and the other linemen around to create favorable matchups. And the DC does it with the type of passion that has his players willing to sacrifice so someone else can get the glory.

 

 "He's energetic, funny, but when it's time to work, he's dialed in," said rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton , who has two sacks this season. "But he's a player's coach. He loves every single one of us and he comes out there like this is his last day."

 The 49ers still have plenty to figure out. While they've limited the big plays, they've struggled to get off the field at times, ranking 24th in the NFL in opponent's time of possession (31:02). They're also 20th in defensive success rate.

 But Brown and his teammates believe that those adjustments will come in time. For most recent 49ers defensive coordinators, time hasn't been an available luxury. After a season, they either moved up to head coaching jobs (Saleh and Ryans) or the Niners moved on from them (Steve Wilks and Nick Sorensen).

 Shanahan hopes that the musical chairs at defensive coordinator will end with Morris. Or, at minimum, slow down dramatically.

 "I see Raheem here for as long as I'm here," Shanahan said. "Raheem's so good of a coach, you've always got to be nervous you'll lose him as a head coach. But if that doesn't happen, I don't plan on him ever leaving."
